From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Exceptional Tyrannosaurus rex fossil

Sue[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/82/FMNH_SUE_Trex.jpg/250px-FMNH_SUE_Trex.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:FMNH_SUE_Trex.jpg)

Sue on display in the [Field Museum of Natural History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_Museum_of_Natural_History "Field Museum of Natural History"), [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago "Chicago") (with some bones reconstructed)
Catalog no.FMNH PR 2081
Common name Sue
Species _[Tyrannosaurus rex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus\_rex "Tyrannosaurus rex")_
Age c. 67 million years[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-sue-1) (aged c.33)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-:3-2)
Place discovered[Cheyenne River Indian Reservation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheyenne_River_Indian_Reservation "Cheyenne River Indian Reservation"), [South Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Dakota "South Dakota"), U.S.
Date discovered August 12, 1990
Discovered by[Susan Hendrickson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_Hendrickson "Sue Hendrickson")

**Sue**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-SUE-3) (stylized: SUE), officially designated [FMNH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_Museum_of_Natural_History "Field Museum of Natural History") PR 2081, is one of the largest,[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-6) most extensive, and best preserved _[Tyrannosaurus rex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus\_rex "Tyrannosaurus rex")_[fossils](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fossil "Fossil") ever found, at over 90% recovered by bulk.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-7)

FMNH PR 2081 was discovered on August 12, 1990,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-8) by [American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") explorer and fossil collector [Sue Hendrickson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_Hendrickson "Sue Hendrickson"), after whom it is named. After ownership disputes were settled, Sue was auctioned in October 1997 for US$8.3 million (equivalent to about $17 million in 2025),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-inflation-US-9) at that time the highest price ever paid for a fossil, and still [among the highest prices paid for a dinosaur skeleton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_dinosaur_specimens_sold_at_auction "List of dinosaur specimens sold at auction"). Sue is now a permanent feature at the [Field Museum of Natural History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_Museum_of_Natural_History "Field Museum of Natural History") in [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago "Chicago"), [Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois "Illinois").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-10)

## Discovery

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sue_(dinosaur)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Discovery")]

During the summer of 1990, a group of workers from the [Black Hills Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Hills_Institute "Black Hills Institute"), located in [Hill City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hill_City,_South_Dakota "Hill City, South Dakota"), searched for fossils at the [Cheyenne River Indian Reservation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheyenne_River_Indian_Reservation "Cheyenne River Indian Reservation") in western [South Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Dakota "South Dakota") near the city of [Faith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith,_South_Dakota "Faith, South Dakota"). By the end of the summer, the group had discovered _[Edmontosaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmontosaurus "Edmontosaurus")_ bones and was ready to leave.

However, a flat tire was discovered on their truck before the group could depart on August 12.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-Steve_Fiffer_2000_-_Ch.1-11)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-12) While the rest of the group went into town to repair the truck, [Sue Hendrickson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_Hendrickson "Sue Hendrickson") decided to explore the nearby cliffs that the group had not checked. As she was walking along the base of a cliff, she discovered some small pieces of bone.

She looked above her to see where the bones had originated, and observed larger bones protruding from the wall of the cliff. She returned to camp with two small pieces of the bones and reported the discovery to the president of the Black Hills Institute, [Peter Larson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Larson "Peter Larson").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-13) He determined that the bones were from a _T.rex_ by their distinctive contour and texture. Later, closer examination of the site showed many visible bones above the ground and some articulated vertebrae.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-Larson-14)[_[page needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing\_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources")_]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/86/SUE_Trex_Real_Bones.jpg/250px-SUE_Trex_Real_Bones.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:SUE_Trex_Real_Bones.jpg)

Highlighted green are the real fossilized bones. The real skull is displayed separately.

The crew ordered extra plaster and, although some of the crew had to depart, Hendrickson and a few other workers began to uncover the bones. The group was excited, as it was evident that much of the dinosaur had been preserved. Previously discovered _T.rex_ skeletons were usually missing over half of their bones.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-Larson-14)

It was later determined that Sue was a record 90% complete by bulk,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-15) and 73% complete counting the elements.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-16) Of the 360 known _T.rex_ bones, around 250 have been recovered.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-sue-1) Scientists believe that this specimen was covered by water and mud soon after its death, which prevented other animals from carrying away the bones.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-Relf-17)[_[page needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing\_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources")_] Additionally, the rushing water mixed the skeleton together.

When the fossil was found, the hip bones were above the skull and the leg bones were intertwined with the ribs. The large size and the excellent condition of the bones were also surprising. The skull was 1.394 m (4 ft 6.9 in) long, and most of the teeth were still intact. After the group completed excavating the bones, each block was covered in [burlap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlap "Burlap") and coated in [plaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plaster "Plaster"), followed by a transfer to the offices of the Black Hills Institute, where they began to clean the bones.

## Dispute and auction

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sue_(dinosaur)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Dispute and auction")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2d/Sue_skull.jpg/250px-Sue_skull.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sue_skull.jpg)

Sue's skull

Soon after the fossil was found, a dispute arose over legal ownership. The Black Hills Institute had obtained permission from the owner of the land, Maurice Williams, to excavate and remove the skeleton, and had paid Williams US$5,000 for the remains.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-18)

Williams later claimed that the money had not been for the sale of the fossil and that he had only allowed Larson to remove and clean the fossil for a later sale.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-Larson-14)[_[page needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing\_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources")_] Williams was a member of the [Sioux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sioux "Sioux") tribe, and the tribe claimed the bones belonged to them. However, the property where the fossil had been found was held in trust by the [United States Department of the Interior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_the_Interior "United States Department of the Interior").

In 1992, the [FBI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Bureau_of_Investigation "Federal Bureau of Investigation") and the [South Dakota National Guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Dakota_National_Guard "South Dakota National Guard") raided the site where the Black Hills Institute had been cleaning the bones and seized the fossil,[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-19) charging Larson on 158 points. The government transferred the remains to the [South Dakota School of Mines and Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Dakota_School_of_Mines_and_Technology "South Dakota School of Mines and Technology"), where the skeleton was stored until the penal and civil legal disputes were settled. The [United States Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate") voted to not confirm the appointment of [Kevin Schieffer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Schieffer?action=edit&redlink=1 "Kevin Schieffer (page does not exist)") as [United States Attorney for the District of South Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Attorney_for_the_District_of_South_Dakota "United States Attorney for the District of South Dakota") after his controversial handling of the penal case.

In 1996, Larson was sentenced to a two-year prison sentence involving customs violations unrelated to the _T.rex_. After a lengthy civil case, the court decreed that Maurice Williams retained ownership.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-20) Williams then decided to sell the remains and contracted with [Sotheby's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sotheby's "Sotheby's") to auction the specimen.

Many at the time worried that the fossil would end up in a private collection where people would not be able to observe it.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-21)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-22)[The Field Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_Museum_of_Natural_History "Field Museum of Natural History") in [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago,_Illinois "Chicago, Illinois") was also concerned about this possibility, and decided to attempt to purchase it. However, the organization realized that they might have had difficulty securing funding and requested that companies and private citizens provide financial support. The [California State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_State_University "California State University") system, [Walt Disney Parks and Resorts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walt_Disney_Parks_and_Resorts "Walt Disney Parks and Resorts"), [McDonald's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McDonald's "McDonald's"), [Ronald McDonald House Charities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_McDonald_House_Charities "Ronald McDonald House Charities"), and individual donors agreed to assist in purchasing Sue for the Field Museum.

On October 4, 1997, the auction began at US$500,000; less than ten minutes later, the Field Museum had purchased the remains with the highest bid of US$7.6 million, which eclipsed bids made on behalf of the [Smithsonian's National Museum of Natural History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_Natural_History "National Museum of Natural History") and the [North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Carolina_Museum_of_Natural_Sciences "North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences"). The final cost was US$8,362,500, making it the most expensive fossil ever sold up until that time.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-23)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-24)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-25) Sue remains one of the [most expensive dinosaur fossils ever sold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_dinosaur_specimens_sold_at_auction "List of dinosaur specimens sold at auction"), only surpassed in 2020 with the sale of _[Stan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan\_(dinosaur) "Stan (dinosaur)")_ the _T.rex_. for $31.8 million, and subsequently in 2024 by [Apex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apex_(dinosaur) "Apex (dinosaur)") the _[Stegosaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stegosaurus "Stegosaurus")_, which sold for $44.6 million. And yet again in 2026 by a different Tyrannosaur by the name of Gus who sold for $50.1 million.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-26)

## Preparation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sue_(dinosaur)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Preparation")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2e/Field_fg06.jpg/250px-Field_fg06.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Field_fg06.jpg)

Field Museum Fossil Preparation Lab

The Field Museum hired a specialized moving company with experience in transporting delicate items to move the bones to Chicago. The truck arrived at the museum in October 1997. Two new research laboratories funded by McDonald's were created and staffed by Field Museum preparators whose job was to slowly and carefully remove all the rock, or "matrix", from the bones. One preparation lab was at the Field Museum itself, the other was at the newly opened [Animal Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disney's_Animal_Kingdom "Disney's Animal Kingdom") in [Disney World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disney_World "Disney World") in Orlando. Millions of visitors observed the preparation of Sue's bones through glass windows in both labs. Footage of the work was also put on the museum's website.

Several of the fossil's bones had never been discovered, so preparators produced models of the missing bones from [plastic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plastic "Plastic") to complete the exhibit. The modeled bones were colored in a purplish hue so that visitors could observe which bones were real and which bones were plastic. The preparators also poured molds of each bone. All the molds were sent to a company outside Toronto to be cast in hollow plastic. The Field Museum kept one set of disarticulated casts in its research collection. The other sets were incorporated into mounted cast skeletons. One set of the casts was sent to [Disney's Animal Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disney's_Animal_Kingdom "Disney's Animal Kingdom") in [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida") to be presented for public display. Two other mounted casts were placed into a traveling tour that was sponsored by the McDonald's Corporation.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-Relf-17)[_[page needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing\_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources")_]

Once the preparators finished removing the matrix from each bone, it was sent to the museum's photographer who made high-quality photographs. From there, the museum's paleontologists began the study of the skeleton. In addition to photographing and studying each bone, the research staff also arranged for [CT scanning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X-ray_computed_tomography "X-ray computed tomography") of select bones. The skull was too large to fit into a medical CT scanner, so [Boeing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing "Boeing")'s Rocketdyne laboratory in California agreed to let the museum use their CT scanner that was normally used to inspect space shuttle parts.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-27)

## Life and death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sue_(dinosaur)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Life and death")]

### Bone damage

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sue_(dinosaur)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Bone damage")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7f/Tyrannosaurus_Sue_skeletal_reconstruction.png/250px-Tyrannosaurus_Sue_skeletal_reconstruction.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tyrannosaurus_Sue_skeletal_reconstruction.png)

Skeletal reconstruction of Sue

Close examination of the bones revealed that Sue was 27–33 years old[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-:3-2) at the time of death (with 33 years old being the best-supported estimate in this range), making it the oldest known _T.rex_ specimen currently published. This was originally estimated as 28 years old,[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-28)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-29) with a later analysis updating the age estimate.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-:3-2) In 2026, Woodward, Myhrvold, and Horner performed a comprehensive histological analysis of 17 tyrannosaur specimens including Sue, and argued that _Tyrannosaurus_ likely experienced a more gradual annual growth rate slope than indicated by earlier studies and evidence of a protracted subadult stage, reaching asymptotic size at around 35–40 years of age. The authors found Sue itself spent at least 11 years at its adult size before dying.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-30)

During its life, Sue suffered from several injuries,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-Relf-17) including a damaged right shoulder blade, a [torn tendon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tendon_avulsion "Tendon avulsion") in the right arm most likely due to a struggle with prey, and three broken ribs.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-rothschild-2001-31) This damage subsequently healed (though one rib healed into two separate pieces), indicating Sue survived the incident.

Sue also suffered numerous other health afflictions. The fossil's left [fibula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fibula "Fibula") is twice the diameter of the right one, likely the result of an infection. Originally the deformity was believed to be from a healed fracture, before later CT scans showed none.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-32) Both the misshapen left fibula and the fused c26 and c27 caudal [vertebrae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertebrae "Vertebrae") show signs consistent with the bone infection [osteomyelitis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osteomyelitis "Osteomyelitis").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-33) Several of Sue's tail vertebrae are fused in a pattern typical of [arthritis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthritis "Arthritis") due to injury. The animal is also believed to have suffered from [gout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gout "Gout").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-Rothschild-34)

Several holes in the front of Sue's skull were originally thought to be either from an infection or bite marks by another tyrannosaur. A 2009 study found these holes to be areas of parasitic infection, possibly from an infestation of an ancestral form of _[Trichomonas gallinae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichomonas\_gallinae "Trichomonas gallinae")_, a protozoan parasite that infests birds and ultimately leads to death by starvation due to internal swelling of the neck.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-35)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-36) Damage to the back end of the skull was interpreted early on as a fatal bite wound, but subsequent study by Field Museum paleontologists found no bite marks. The distortion and breakage seen in some of the bones in the back of the skull was likely caused by post-mortem trampling.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Sue's cause of death is ultimately unknown.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-Larson-14)[_[page needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing\_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources")_] The dinosaur died in a seasonal stream bed, which washed away some small bones as it rapidly covered the remains with sediment, ultimately leading to [fossilization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fossilization "Fossilization").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-:0-37)

### Size

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sue_(dinosaur)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Size")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c3/Tyrannosaurus_specimens.svg/330px-Tyrannosaurus_specimens.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tyrannosaurus_specimens.svg)

"Sue" and other specimens to scale with a human

Sue is approximately 12.3–12.8 meters (40.4–42.0 ft) long along the centra, and stands 3.66–3.96 meters (12–13 ft) tall at the hips.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-Hutchinsonet.al.2011-38)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-SueFMNH-39)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-sue-1) Sue is one of the largest _Tyrannosaurus_ specimens, only possibly exceeded by [Scotty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotty_(dinosaur) "Scotty (dinosaur)") (RSM P2523.8).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-Persons-4)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-40)

Sue possesses the longest known [gastralium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gastralium "Gastralium") (belly rib) among theropods, measuring about 90 centimeters (3.0 ft). Sue also has the longest known [pubis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pubis_(bone) "Pubis (bone)") currently measured among the Cretaceous theropods, measuring roughly 136 centimeters (4.46 ft).

### Weight

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sue_(dinosaur)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Weight")]

Sue has been estimated to have weighed between 8.4–14 metric tons (9.26–15.4 [short tons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short_ton "Short ton")) when living, as of 2018.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-HartmanMassEstimate-41)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-Holtz2008-42)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-SueFMNH-39)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-FMNH-43) In 2011, other weight estimates were between 5,560–10,011 kilograms (6.13–11.0 [short tons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short_ton "Short ton")), although the authors stated that their upper and lower estimates were based on models with wide possible errors, and that they "consider them [these extremes] to be too skinny, too fat, or too disproportionate".[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-Hutchinsonet.al.2011-38) A further estimate portrayed a leaner build, placing the specimen at 8.4 metric tons (9.3 short tons),[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-HartmanMassEstimate-41) while older estimates have placed this specimen at 5.7–6.4 metric tons (6.3–7.1 short tons) in weight.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-ericksonetal2004-44)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-vital-45) A study conducted back in 2014 that estimated the weight for some of the large theropod dinosaurs and both Sue and Scotty were included. This older study concluded that Sue was around 7,377 kg (8.1 tons) with a weight range of 5,531 kg (6 tons) to 9,224 kg (10 tons) while Scotty was heavier at 8,004 kg (8.8 tons) with a weight range of 6,000 kg (6.6 tons) to 10,007 kg (11 tons).[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-46)

Displayed separately from the whole body, the skull weighs 272 kg (600 lb).[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-vital-45)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-Skull_Weight-47)

## Exhibition

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sue_(dinosaur)&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Exhibition")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/44/Field_Museum_August_2010_1_%28Sue%29.JPG/250px-Field_Museum_August_2010_1_%28Sue%29.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Field_Museum_August_2010_1_(Sue).JPG)

Sue as originally mounted in Stanley Field Hall

Following preparation, photography, and study, the bones were sent to New Jersey[_[when?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers#Chronological\_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_] where work began on making the mount. Sue's mount consists of a bent steel frame which supports each bone safely, displaying the skeleton fully articulated as it was in life.

The dinosaur's real skull was not incorporated into the mounted display, as subsequent study would be difficult with the head 4 m (13 ft) off the ground. Additionally, parts of the skull had been crushed and broken and thus appeared distorted.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-:1-48) The museum made a cast of the skull, and altered this cast to remove the distortions, thus approximating what the original undistorted skull may have looked like. The cast skull was also lighter, allowing it to be displayed on the mount without the use of a steel upright under the head. The original skull was exhibited in a separate case, which could be opened to allow researchers access for study.

Originally, the Field Museum had plans to incorporate Sue into their preexisting dinosaur exhibit on the second floor, but had little left in their budget to do so after purchasing it. Instead, the _T.rex_ was put on display in the building's main hall directly in front of the museum's north entrance, where it would remain for the next 18 years.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-49)

Sue was unveiled on May 17, 2000, attracting over 10,000 visitors that day.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-50)[John Gurche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Gurche "John Gurche"), a [paleoartist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paleoart "Paleoart"), painted a mural of a _Tyrannosaurus_ for the exhibit.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-51)

### New suite (2019)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sue_(dinosaur)&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: New suite (2019)")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/SUE_FM_2081_T_rex_furcula.jpg/250px-SUE_FM_2081_T_rex_furcula.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:SUE_FM_2081_T_rex_furcula.jpg)

With the correct furcula in place, the shoulders are lowered and meet in the middle of the chest– bringing the arms closer to the ground.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-52)

In early 2018, Sue was dismantled and moved to its own gallery on the museum's upper level, connected to the _Evolving Planet_ exhibit and the Elizabeth Morse Genius Hall of Dinosaurs.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-53) The new exhibit opened on December 21, 2018.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-54)

The 5,100-square-foot (470 m 2) exhibit includes animated videos of Sue that are projected in [6K](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/6K_resolution "6K resolution") onto nine-foot tall panes behind its skeleton.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-55)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-:1-48)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-:2-56) Atlantic Productions worked with the Field Museum to create multiple animated sequences, including Sue scavenging an _[Ankylosaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ankylosaurus "Ankylosaurus")_ carcass, battling a _[Triceratops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triceratops "Triceratops")_, and hunting an _[Edmontosaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmontosaurus "Edmontosaurus")_.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-:2-56)

According to the Field Museum's associate curator of dinosaurs Pete Makovicky, the new suite was designed to accentuate the size and stature of Sue, and although smaller, the exhibit allows for a more intimate display of the _T.rex_,[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-57) along with the skull of a _[Triceratops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triceratops "Triceratops")_ and other Cretaceous period artifacts, such as shark teeth and [pachycephalosaurid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pachycephalosauria "Pachycephalosauria") bones.

Sue's reassembled display is intended to reflect the newest scientific theories, including the proper [furcula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Furcula "Furcula") and attachment of the [gastralia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gastralia "Gastralia") to the rest of the skeleton.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-PressRelease20180130-58)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-59)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-60)

Sue's real skull is kept in a separate display case in the exhibition, allowing it to be removed for study as required.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-:1-48)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-61)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-:2-56)

## _Tyrannosaurus imperator_ debate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sue_(dinosaur)&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Tyrannosaurus imperator debate")]

In a 2022 study, [Gregory S. Paul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregory_S._Paul "Gregory S. Paul") and colleagues argued that _Tyrannosaurus rex_, as traditionally understood, actually represents three species: the type species _Tyrannosaurus rex_, and two new species: _T.imperator_ (meaning "tyrant lizard emperor") and _T.regina_ (meaning "tyrant lizard queen"). The [holotype](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holotype "Holotype") of the former (_T.imperator_) is the Sue specimen, and the holotype of the latter (_T.regina_) is [Wankel rex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wankel_rex "Wankel rex"). Paul interpreted Sue to represent an earlier population of _Tyrannosaurus_, which [speciated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speciation "Speciation") into _T.rex_ and _T.regina_.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-paul2022-62)

However, the majority of paleontologists who have extensively studied the clade expressed skepticism or criticized the study’s methodology and conclusions in mass media. Critics included [Stephen Brusatte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Brusatte "Stephen Brusatte"), [Thomas Carr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Carr_(paleontologist) "Thomas Carr (paleontologist)"), [Thomas Holtz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Holtz "Thomas Holtz"), David Hone, [Jingmai O'Connor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jingmai_O'Connor "Jingmai O'Connor"), and [Lindsay Zanno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindsay_Zanno "Lindsay Zanno").[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-newyorktimes-63)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-64)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-65) Their criticism was subsequently published in a technical paper.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-Carr_et.al.(2022)-66) Holtz remarked that, even if _Tyrannosaurus imperator_ represented a distinct species from _Tyrannosaurus rex_, it may represent the same species as _Nanotyrannus lancensis_ and would need to be called _Tyrannosaurus lancensis_. O'Connor, a curator at the Field Museum, where the _T.imperator_ holotype Sue is displayed, regarded the new species as too poorly supported to justify modifying the exhibit signs.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-newyorktimes-63)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Exceptional Tyrannosaurus rex fossil

Sue[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/82/FMNH_SUE_Trex.jpg/250px-FMNH_SUE_Trex.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:FMNH_SUE_Trex.jpg)

Sue on display in the [Field Museum of Natural History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_Museum_of_Natural_History "Field Museum of Natural History"), [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago "Chicago") (with some bones reconstructed)
Catalog no.FMNH PR 2081
Common name Sue
Species _[Tyrannosaurus rex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus\_rex "Tyrannosaurus rex")_
Age c. 67 million years[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-sue-1) (aged c.33)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-:3-2)
Place discovered[Cheyenne River Indian Reservation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheyenne_River_Indian_Reservation "Cheyenne River Indian Reservation"), [South Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Dakota "South Dakota"), U.S.
Date discovered August 12, 1990
Discovered by[Susan Hendrickson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_Hendrickson "Sue Hendrickson")

**Sue**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-SUE-3) (stylized: SUE), officially designated [FMNH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_Museum_of_Natural_History "Field Museum of Natural History") PR 2081, is one of the largest,[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-6) most extensive, and best preserved _[Tyrannosaurus rex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus\_rex "Tyrannosaurus rex")_[fossils](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fossil "Fossil") ever found, at over 90% recovered by bulk.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-7)

FMNH PR 2081 was discovered on August 12, 1990,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-8) by [American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") explorer and fossil collector [Sue Hendrickson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_Hendrickson "Sue Hendrickson"), after whom it is named. After ownership disputes were settled, Sue was auctioned in October 1997 for US$8.3 million (equivalent to about $17 million in 2025),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-inflation-US-9) at that time the highest price ever paid for a fossil, and still [among the highest prices paid for a dinosaur skeleton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_dinosaur_specimens_sold_at_auction "List of dinosaur specimens sold at auction"). Sue is now a permanent feature at the [Field Museum of Natural History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_Museum_of_Natural_History "Field Museum of Natural History") in [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago "Chicago"), [Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois "Illinois").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-10)

## Discovery

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sue_(dinosaur)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Discovery")]

During the summer of 1990, a group of workers from the [Black Hills Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Hills_Institute "Black Hills Institute"), located in [Hill City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hill_City,_South_Dakota "Hill City, South Dakota"), searched for fossils at the [Cheyenne River Indian Reservation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheyenne_River_Indian_Reservation "Cheyenne River Indian Reservation") in western [South Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Dakota "South Dakota") near the city of [Faith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith,_South_Dakota "Faith, South Dakota"). By the end of the summer, the group had discovered _[Edmontosaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmontosaurus "Edmontosaurus")_ bones and was ready to leave.

However, a flat tire was discovered on their truck before the group could depart on August 12.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-Steve_Fiffer_2000_-_Ch.1-11)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-12) While the rest of the group went into town to repair the truck, [Sue Hendrickson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_Hendrickson "Sue Hendrickson") decided to explore the nearby cliffs that the group had not checked. As she was walking along the base of a cliff, she discovered some small pieces of bone.

She looked above her to see where the bones had originated, and observed larger bones protruding from the wall of the cliff. She returned to camp with two small pieces of the bones and reported the discovery to the president of the Black Hills Institute, [Peter Larson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Larson "Peter Larson").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-13) He determined that the bones were from a _T.rex_ by their distinctive contour and texture. Later, closer examination of the site showed many visible bones above the ground and some articulated vertebrae.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-Larson-14)[_[page needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing\_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources")_]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/86/SUE_Trex_Real_Bones.jpg/250px-SUE_Trex_Real_Bones.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:SUE_Trex_Real_Bones.jpg)

Highlighted green are the real fossilized bones. The real skull is displayed separately.

The crew ordered extra plaster and, although some of the crew had to depart, Hendrickson and a few other workers began to uncover the bones. The group was excited, as it was evident that much of the dinosaur had been preserved. Previously discovered _T.rex_ skeletons were usually missing over half of their bones.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-Larson-14)

It was later determined that Sue was a record 90% complete by bulk,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-15) and 73% complete counting the elements.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-16) Of the 360 known _T.rex_ bones, around 250 have been recovered.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-sue-1) Scientists believe that this specimen was covered by water and mud soon after its death, which prevented other animals from carrying away the bones.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-Relf-17)[_[page needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing\_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources")_] Additionally, the rushing water mixed the skeleton together.

When the fossil was found, the hip bones were above the skull and the leg bones were intertwined with the ribs. The large size and the excellent condition of the bones were also surprising. The skull was 1.394 m (4 ft 6.9 in) long, and most of the teeth were still intact. After the group completed excavating the bones, each block was covered in [burlap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlap "Burlap") and coated in [plaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plaster "Plaster"), followed by a transfer to the offices of the Black Hills Institute, where they began to clean the bones.

## Dispute and auction

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sue_(dinosaur)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Dispute and auction")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2d/Sue_skull.jpg/250px-Sue_skull.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sue_skull.jpg)

Sue's skull

Soon after the fossil was found, a dispute arose over legal ownership. The Black Hills Institute had obtained permission from the owner of the land, Maurice Williams, to excavate and remove the skeleton, and had paid Williams US$5,000 for the remains.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-18)

Williams later claimed that the money had not been for the sale of the fossil and that he had only allowed Larson to remove and clean the fossil for a later sale.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-Larson-14)[_[page needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing\_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources")_] Williams was a member of the [Sioux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sioux "Sioux") tribe, and the tribe claimed the bones belonged to them. However, the property where the fossil had been found was held in trust by the [United States Department of the Interior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_the_Interior "United States Department of the Interior").

In 1992, the [FBI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Bureau_of_Investigation "Federal Bureau of Investigation") and the [South Dakota National Guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Dakota_National_Guard "South Dakota National Guard") raided the site where the Black Hills Institute had been cleaning the bones and seized the fossil,[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-19) charging Larson on 158 points. The government transferred the remains to the [South Dakota School of Mines and Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Dakota_School_of_Mines_and_Technology "South Dakota School of Mines and Technology"), where the skeleton was stored until the penal and civil legal disputes were settled. The [United States Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate") voted to not confirm the appointment of [Kevin Schieffer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Schieffer?action=edit&redlink=1 "Kevin Schieffer (page does not exist)") as [United States Attorney for the District of South Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Attorney_for_the_District_of_South_Dakota "United States Attorney for the District of South Dakota") after his controversial handling of the penal case.

In 1996, Larson was sentenced to a two-year prison sentence involving customs violations unrelated to the _T.rex_. After a lengthy civil case, the court decreed that Maurice Williams retained ownership.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-20) Williams then decided to sell the remains and contracted with [Sotheby's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sotheby's "Sotheby's") to auction the specimen.

Many at the time worried that the fossil would end up in a private collection where people would not be able to observe it.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-21)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-22)[The Field Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_Museum_of_Natural_History "Field Museum of Natural History") in [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago,_Illinois "Chicago, Illinois") was also concerned about this possibility, and decided to attempt to purchase it. However, the organization realized that they might have had difficulty securing funding and requested that companies and private citizens provide financial support. The [California State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_State_University "California State University") system, [Walt Disney Parks and Resorts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walt_Disney_Parks_and_Resorts "Walt Disney Parks and Resorts"), [McDonald's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McDonald's "McDonald's"), [Ronald McDonald House Charities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_McDonald_House_Charities "Ronald McDonald House Charities"), and individual donors agreed to assist in purchasing Sue for the Field Museum.

On October 4, 1997, the auction began at US$500,000; less than ten minutes later, the Field Museum had purchased the remains with the highest bid of US$7.6 million, which eclipsed bids made on behalf of the [Smithsonian's National Museum of Natural History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_Natural_History "National Museum of Natural History") and the [North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Carolina_Museum_of_Natural_Sciences "North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences"). The final cost was US$8,362,500, making it the most expensive fossil ever sold up until that time.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-23)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-24)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-25) Sue remains one of the [most expensive dinosaur fossils ever sold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_dinosaur_specimens_sold_at_auction "List of dinosaur specimens sold at auction"), only surpassed in 2020 with the sale of _[Stan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan\_(dinosaur) "Stan (dinosaur)")_ the _T.rex_. for $31.8 million, and subsequently in 2024 by [Apex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apex_(dinosaur) "Apex (dinosaur)") the _[Stegosaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stegosaurus "Stegosaurus")_, which sold for $44.6 million. And yet again in 2026 by a different Tyrannosaur by the name of Gus who sold for $50.1 million.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-26)

## Preparation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sue_(dinosaur)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Preparation")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2e/Field_fg06.jpg/250px-Field_fg06.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Field_fg06.jpg)

Field Museum Fossil Preparation Lab

The Field Museum hired a specialized moving company with experience in transporting delicate items to move the bones to Chicago. The truck arrived at the museum in October 1997. Two new research laboratories funded by McDonald's were created and staffed by Field Museum preparators whose job was to slowly and carefully remove all the rock, or "matrix", from the bones. One preparation lab was at the Field Museum itself, the other was at the newly opened [Animal Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disney's_Animal_Kingdom "Disney's Animal Kingdom") in [Disney World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disney_World "Disney World") in Orlando. Millions of visitors observed the preparation of Sue's bones through glass windows in both labs. Footage of the work was also put on the museum's website.

Several of the fossil's bones had never been discovered, so preparators produced models of the missing bones from [plastic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plastic "Plastic") to complete the exhibit. The modeled bones were colored in a purplish hue so that visitors could observe which bones were real and which bones were plastic. The preparators also poured molds of each bone. All the molds were sent to a company outside Toronto to be cast in hollow plastic. The Field Museum kept one set of disarticulated casts in its research collection. The other sets were incorporated into mounted cast skeletons. One set of the casts was sent to [Disney's Animal Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disney's_Animal_Kingdom "Disney's Animal Kingdom") in [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida") to be presented for public display. Two other mounted casts were placed into a traveling tour that was sponsored by the McDonald's Corporation.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-Relf-17)[_[page needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing\_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources")_]

Once the preparators finished removing the matrix from each bone, it was sent to the museum's photographer who made high-quality photographs. From there, the museum's paleontologists began the study of the skeleton. In addition to photographing and studying each bone, the research staff also arranged for [CT scanning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X-ray_computed_tomography "X-ray computed tomography") of select bones. The skull was too large to fit into a medical CT scanner, so [Boeing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing "Boeing")'s Rocketdyne laboratory in California agreed to let the museum use their CT scanner that was normally used to inspect space shuttle parts.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-27)

## Life and death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sue_(dinosaur)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Life and death")]

### Bone damage

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sue_(dinosaur)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Bone damage")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7f/Tyrannosaurus_Sue_skeletal_reconstruction.png/250px-Tyrannosaurus_Sue_skeletal_reconstruction.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tyrannosaurus_Sue_skeletal_reconstruction.png)

Skeletal reconstruction of Sue

Close examination of the bones revealed that Sue was 27–33 years old[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-:3-2) at the time of death (with 33 years old being the best-supported estimate in this range), making it the oldest known _T.rex_ specimen currently published. This was originally estimated as 28 years old,[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-28)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-29) with a later analysis updating the age estimate.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-:3-2) In 2026, Woodward, Myhrvold, and Horner performed a comprehensive histological analysis of 17 tyrannosaur specimens including Sue, and argued that _Tyrannosaurus_ likely experienced a more gradual annual growth rate slope than indicated by earlier studies and evidence of a protracted subadult stage, reaching asymptotic size at around 35–40 years of age. The authors found Sue itself spent at least 11 years at its adult size before dying.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-30)

During its life, Sue suffered from several injuries,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-Relf-17) including a damaged right shoulder blade, a [torn tendon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tendon_avulsion "Tendon avulsion") in the right arm most likely due to a struggle with prey, and three broken ribs.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-rothschild-2001-31) This damage subsequently healed (though one rib healed into two separate pieces), indicating Sue survived the incident.

Sue also suffered numerous other health afflictions. The fossil's left [fibula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fibula "Fibula") is twice the diameter of the right one, likely the result of an infection. Originally the deformity was believed to be from a healed fracture, before later CT scans showed none.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-32) Both the misshapen left fibula and the fused c26 and c27 caudal [vertebrae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertebrae "Vertebrae") show signs consistent with the bone infection [osteomyelitis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osteomyelitis "Osteomyelitis").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-33) Several of Sue's tail vertebrae are fused in a pattern typical of [arthritis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthritis "Arthritis") due to injury. The animal is also believed to have suffered from [gout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gout "Gout").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-Rothschild-34)

Several holes in the front of Sue's skull were originally thought to be either from an infection or bite marks by another tyrannosaur. A 2009 study found these holes to be areas of parasitic infection, possibly from an infestation of an ancestral form of _[Trichomonas gallinae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichomonas\_gallinae "Trichomonas gallinae")_, a protozoan parasite that infests birds and ultimately leads to death by starvation due to internal swelling of the neck.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-35)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-36) Damage to the back end of the skull was interpreted early on as a fatal bite wound, but subsequent study by Field Museum paleontologists found no bite marks. The distortion and breakage seen in some of the bones in the back of the skull was likely caused by post-mortem trampling.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Sue's cause of death is ultimately unknown.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-Larson-14)[_[page needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing\_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources")_] The dinosaur died in a seasonal stream bed, which washed away some small bones as it rapidly covered the remains with sediment, ultimately leading to [fossilization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fossilization "Fossilization").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-:0-37)

### Size

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sue_(dinosaur)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Size")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c3/Tyrannosaurus_specimens.svg/330px-Tyrannosaurus_specimens.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tyrannosaurus_specimens.svg)

"Sue" and other specimens to scale with a human

Sue is approximately 12.3–12.8 meters (40.4–42.0 ft) long along the centra, and stands 3.66–3.96 meters (12–13 ft) tall at the hips.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-Hutchinsonet.al.2011-38)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-SueFMNH-39)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-sue-1) Sue is one of the largest _Tyrannosaurus_ specimens, only possibly exceeded by [Scotty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotty_(dinosaur) "Scotty (dinosaur)") (RSM P2523.8).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-Persons-4)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-40)

Sue possesses the longest known [gastralium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gastralium "Gastralium") (belly rib) among theropods, measuring about 90 centimeters (3.0 ft). Sue also has the longest known [pubis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pubis_(bone) "Pubis (bone)") currently measured among the Cretaceous theropods, measuring roughly 136 centimeters (4.46 ft).

### Weight

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sue_(dinosaur)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Weight")]

Sue has been estimated to have weighed between 8.4–14 metric tons (9.26–15.4 [short tons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short_ton "Short ton")) when living, as of 2018.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-HartmanMassEstimate-41)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-Holtz2008-42)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-SueFMNH-39)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-FMNH-43) In 2011, other weight estimates were between 5,560–10,011 kilograms (6.13–11.0 [short tons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short_ton "Short ton")), although the authors stated that their upper and lower estimates were based on models with wide possible errors, and that they "consider them [these extremes] to be too skinny, too fat, or too disproportionate".[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-Hutchinsonet.al.2011-38) A further estimate portrayed a leaner build, placing the specimen at 8.4 metric tons (9.3 short tons),[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-HartmanMassEstimate-41) while older estimates have placed this specimen at 5.7–6.4 metric tons (6.3–7.1 short tons) in weight.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-ericksonetal2004-44)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-vital-45) A study conducted back in 2014 that estimated the weight for some of the large theropod dinosaurs and both Sue and Scotty were included. This older study concluded that Sue was around 7,377 kg (8.1 tons) with a weight range of 5,531 kg (6 tons) to 9,224 kg (10 tons) while Scotty was heavier at 8,004 kg (8.8 tons) with a weight range of 6,000 kg (6.6 tons) to 10,007 kg (11 tons).[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-46)

Displayed separately from the whole body, the skull weighs 272 kg (600 lb).[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-vital-45)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-Skull_Weight-47)

## Exhibition

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sue_(dinosaur)&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Exhibition")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/44/Field_Museum_August_2010_1_%28Sue%29.JPG/250px-Field_Museum_August_2010_1_%28Sue%29.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Field_Museum_August_2010_1_(Sue).JPG)

Sue as originally mounted in Stanley Field Hall

Following preparation, photography, and study, the bones were sent to New Jersey[_[when?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers#Chronological\_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_] where work began on making the mount. Sue's mount consists of a bent steel frame which supports each bone safely, displaying the skeleton fully articulated as it was in life.

The dinosaur's real skull was not incorporated into the mounted display, as subsequent study would be difficult with the head 4 m (13 ft) off the ground. Additionally, parts of the skull had been crushed and broken and thus appeared distorted.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-:1-48) The museum made a cast of the skull, and altered this cast to remove the distortions, thus approximating what the original undistorted skull may have looked like. The cast skull was also lighter, allowing it to be displayed on the mount without the use of a steel upright under the head. The original skull was exhibited in a separate case, which could be opened to allow researchers access for study.

Originally, the Field Museum had plans to incorporate Sue into their preexisting dinosaur exhibit on the second floor, but had little left in their budget to do so after purchasing it. Instead, the _T.rex_ was put on display in the building's main hall directly in front of the museum's north entrance, where it would remain for the next 18 years.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-49)

Sue was unveiled on May 17, 2000, attracting over 10,000 visitors that day.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-50)[John Gurche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Gurche "John Gurche"), a [paleoartist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paleoart "Paleoart"), painted a mural of a _Tyrannosaurus_ for the exhibit.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-51)

### New suite (2019)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sue_(dinosaur)&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: New suite (2019)")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/SUE_FM_2081_T_rex_furcula.jpg/250px-SUE_FM_2081_T_rex_furcula.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:SUE_FM_2081_T_rex_furcula.jpg)

With the correct furcula in place, the shoulders are lowered and meet in the middle of the chest– bringing the arms closer to the ground.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-52)

In early 2018, Sue was dismantled and moved to its own gallery on the museum's upper level, connected to the _Evolving Planet_ exhibit and the Elizabeth Morse Genius Hall of Dinosaurs.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-53) The new exhibit opened on December 21, 2018.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-54)

The 5,100-square-foot (470 m 2) exhibit includes animated videos of Sue that are projected in [6K](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/6K_resolution "6K resolution") onto nine-foot tall panes behind its skeleton.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-55)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-:1-48)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-:2-56) Atlantic Productions worked with the Field Museum to create multiple animated sequences, including Sue scavenging an _[Ankylosaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ankylosaurus "Ankylosaurus")_ carcass, battling a _[Triceratops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triceratops "Triceratops")_, and hunting an _[Edmontosaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmontosaurus "Edmontosaurus")_.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-:2-56)

According to the Field Museum's associate curator of dinosaurs Pete Makovicky, the new suite was designed to accentuate the size and stature of Sue, and although smaller, the exhibit allows for a more intimate display of the _T.rex_,[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-57) along with the skull of a _[Triceratops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triceratops "Triceratops")_ and other Cretaceous period artifacts, such as shark teeth and [pachycephalosaurid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pachycephalosauria "Pachycephalosauria") bones.

Sue's reassembled display is intended to reflect the newest scientific theories, including the proper [furcula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Furcula "Furcula") and attachment of the [gastralia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gastralia "Gastralia") to the rest of the skeleton.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-PressRelease20180130-58)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-59)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-60)

Sue's real skull is kept in a separate display case in the exhibition, allowing it to be removed for study as required.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-:1-48)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-61)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-:2-56)

## _Tyrannosaurus imperator_ debate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sue_(dinosaur)&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Tyrannosaurus imperator debate")]

In a 2022 study, [Gregory S. Paul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregory_S._Paul "Gregory S. Paul") and colleagues argued that _Tyrannosaurus rex_, as traditionally understood, actually represents three species: the type species _Tyrannosaurus rex_, and two new species: _T.imperator_ (meaning "tyrant lizard emperor") and _T.regina_ (meaning "tyrant lizard queen"). The [holotype](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holotype "Holotype") of the former (_T.imperator_) is the Sue specimen, and the holotype of the latter (_T.regina_) is [Wankel rex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wankel_rex "Wankel rex"). Paul interpreted Sue to represent an earlier population of _Tyrannosaurus_, which [speciated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speciation "Speciation") into _T.rex_ and _T.regina_.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-paul2022-62)

However, the majority of paleontologists who have extensively studied the clade expressed skepticism or criticized the study’s methodology and conclusions in mass media. Critics included [Stephen Brusatte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Brusatte "Stephen Brusatte"), [Thomas Carr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Carr_(paleontologist) "Thomas Carr (paleontologist)"), [Thomas Holtz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Holtz "Thomas Holtz"), David Hone, [Jingmai O'Connor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jingmai_O'Connor "Jingmai O'Connor"), and [Lindsay Zanno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindsay_Zanno "Lindsay Zanno").[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-newyorktimes-63)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-64)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-65) Their criticism was subsequently published in a technical paper.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-Carr_et.al.(2022)-66) Holtz remarked that, even if _Tyrannosaurus imperator_ represented a distinct species from _Tyrannosaurus rex_, it may represent the same species as _Nanotyrannus lancensis_ and would need to be called _Tyrannosaurus lancensis_. O'Connor, a curator at the Field Museum, where the _T.imperator_ holotype Sue is displayed, regarded the new species as too poorly supported to justify modifying the exhibit signs.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-newyorktimes-63)

Sue's discovery and the subsequent legal battles were featured in Director [Todd Miller's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Todd_Douglas_Miller "Todd Douglas Miller") documentary _[Dinosaur 13](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinosaur\_13 "Dinosaur 13")_, which premiered at the 2014 [Sundance Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sundance_Film_Festival "Sundance Film Festival")[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-70) and was subsequently released in theaters and on DVD.

In 2015, an episode of [NPR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NPR "NPR")'s _[Planet Money](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planet\_Money "Planet Money")_ discussed the acquisition of Sue from a financial and legal perspective.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur)#cite_note-Planet_Money-71)

**Susan Hendrickson** (born December 2, 1949) is an American explorer and fossil collector. Hendrickson is best known for her discovery of the remains of a _[Tyrannosaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus "Tyrannosaurus") rex_ in [South Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Dakota "South Dakota") on August 12, 1990, in the Cheyenne River Reservation. Her discovery is the most complete skeleton of _Tyrannosaurus_ known to science. This skeleton is now known as "[Sue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur) "Sue (dinosaur)")" in honor of her. It is on display at the [Field Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_Museum "Field Museum") in Chicago, Illinois. She has also found other important [fossils](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fossils "Fossils") and [artifacts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artifact_(archaeology) "Artifact (archaeology)") around the world.

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sue_Hendrickson&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Hendrickson was born in Chicago, Illinois, to Lee and Mary Hendrickson; her family soon moved to nearby [Munster, Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munster,_Indiana "Munster, Indiana"), where she grew up.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_Hendrickson#cite_note-Gaines15-1) She has two siblings: an older brother, John,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_Hendrickson#cite_note-Gaines16-2) and her younger sister, Karen. Her father was a successful railroad purchasing agent, while her mother worked at [American Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Airlines "American Airlines").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_Hendrickson#cite_note-Gaines16-2)

In 1955, Hendrickson was enrolled at Munster's public elementary school, frequently being praised by her teachers as "a good student and obedient child".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_Hendrickson#cite_note-Gaines17-3) However, she eventually found herself bored with school in Munster, and at age 16 was able to convince her parents to let her stay with her aunt in Florida, where she enrolled at a [Fort Lauderdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Lauderdale,_Florida "Fort Lauderdale, Florida") high school. An adventurous and rebellious teenager, Hendrickson never completed high school, dropping out at the age of 17 in favor of moving from state to state with her boyfriend before settling in Florida, where she was hired by two professional divers who ran an aquarium fish business.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_Hendrickson#cite_note-Gaines23-4) A strong swimmer who had once been on her high school's swim team, Hendrickson quickly learned to dive and began collecting tropical fish off the [Florida Keys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida_Keys "Florida Keys") to sell to [aquarists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquarists "Aquarists") and pet stores.

Aside from her work as a diver, Hendrickson also worked part of the year as a lobster fisherman, and would occasionally take the summer off to volunteer on paleontological digs. She later moved to [Seattle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle "Seattle"), earned her [GED](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Equivalency_Diploma "General Equivalency Diploma"), and considered enrolling at the [University of Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Washington "University of Washington") in order to pursue a [marine biology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_biology "Marine biology") degree, but decided against it, leaving Seattle after a year and moving back to Florida to pursue her diving career.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_Hendrickson#cite_note-Gaines26-5)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sue_Hendrickson&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

In 1970, Hendrickson had a large circle of friends in the diving business, and one day was invited to participate in a [salvage diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wreck_diving "Wreck diving") expedition off the Florida Keys, which she eagerly undertook. Her job was to retrieve valuable building materials that were stored in a cargo freighter which ran aground on a [coral reef](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coral_reef "Coral reef").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_Hendrickson#cite_note-Gaines29-6) While continuing her work in salvage, Hendrickson soon found herself exploring old shipwrecks, later going to the [Dominican Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominican_Republic "Dominican Republic"). She was fascinated by working in the company of archaeologists and fell in love with the country, visiting the island often.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_Hendrickson#cite_note-Gaines35-7)

By the mid-1980s, Hendrickson had also attempted mining [amber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominican_amber "Dominican amber") in the Dominican mountains. She had become one of the largest amber providers for scientists. Hendrickson also found three perfect 23-million-year-old butterflies, which make up a half of the whole world's total collection. Although she found the work too monotonous to pursue full-time, writing that "You could dig for months and find nothing in the Dominican caves,"[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_Hendrickson#cite_note-Gaines37-8) she continued studying [paleo entomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entomology "Entomology"), becoming an expert at identifying fossilized insects.

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fc/Sues_skeleton.jpg/250px-Sues_skeleton.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sues_skeleton.jpg)

[_T. rex_ specimen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur) "Sue (dinosaur)") discovered by Sue Hendrickson

She also met Swiss paleontologist Kirby Siber, who allowed her to join his team consisting of paleontologists Carlos Martin and [Peter Larson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Larson "Peter Larson").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_Hendrickson#cite_note-Gaines41-9) The group began excavating [Miocene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miocene_epoch "Miocene epoch")[baleen whale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baleen_whale "Baleen whale") fossils at an ancient seabed in Peru, and Hendrickson joined the team for several summers, discovering fossilized dolphins, whales, and sharks.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_Hendrickson#cite_note-Gaines41-9) She later accompanied Larson to the [Black Hills Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Hills_Institute "Black Hills Institute") in South Dakota. By this time, paleontology had become her main passion.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_Hendrickson#cite_note-Gaines44-10) On August 12, 1990, while examining a cliff-side in South Dakota with a team from the Black Hills Institute, she discovered a _Tyrannosaurus rex_ specimen – the largest, most complete, and best preserved _T. rex_ ever found. The specimen was later named "[Sue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur) "Sue (dinosaur)")" in her honor.

In 1992, Hendrickson joined a team of marine [archaeologists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology "Archaeology") headed by [Franck Goddio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franck_Goddio "Franck Goddio"). With them, she took part in many diving expeditions, the most notable of which were the Royal Quarters of [Cleopatra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleopatra_VII "Cleopatra VII"), and [Napoleon Bonaparte's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleon_I_of_France "Napoleon I of France") lost fleet from the [Battle of the Nile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Nile "Battle of the Nile").

In 2005, [_Glamour_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glamour_(magazine) "Glamour (magazine)") magazine honored her in their "Glamour Woman of the Year Awards". In 2001, she published an autobiography entitled _Hunt for the Past: My Life as an Explorer_ (New York, NY: Scholastic, Inc). In 2008, she was featured on the "Dare to Explore" chapter of _[National Geographic Kids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National\_Geographic\_Kids "National Geographic Kids")_.

Hendrickson now[_[when?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers#Chronological\_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_] lives on the island of [Guanaja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guanaja "Guanaja"), off the coast of [Honduras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honduras "Honduras"). She is a member of the [Paleontological Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paleontological_Society "Paleontological Society"), [Explorers Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Explorers_Club "The Explorers Club"), [Society for Historical Archaeology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Society_for_Historical_Archaeology "Society for Historical Archaeology"), and was awarded an [honorary Ph.D.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honorary_doctorate "Honorary doctorate") from the [University of Illinois at Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago "University of Illinois at Chicago") in 2000.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_Hendrickson#cite_note-officialsite-11)
