**Susan Hendrickson** (born December 2, 1949) is an American explorer and fossil collector. Hendrickson is best known for her discovery of the remains of a _[Tyrannosaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus "Tyrannosaurus") rex_ in [South Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Dakota "South Dakota") on August 12, 1990, in the Cheyenne River Reservation. Her discovery is the most complete skeleton of _Tyrannosaurus_ known to science. This skeleton is now known as "[Sue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur) "Sue (dinosaur)")" in honor of her. It is on display at the [Field Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_Museum "Field Museum") in Chicago, Illinois. She has also found other important [fossils](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fossils "Fossils") and [artifacts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artifact_(archaeology) "Artifact (archaeology)") around the world.

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sue_Hendrickson&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Hendrickson was born in Chicago, Illinois, to Lee and Mary Hendrickson; her family soon moved to nearby [Munster, Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munster,_Indiana "Munster, Indiana"), where she grew up.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_Hendrickson#cite_note-Gaines15-1) She has two siblings: an older brother, John,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_Hendrickson#cite_note-Gaines16-2) and her younger sister, Karen. Her father was a successful railroad purchasing agent, while her mother worked at [American Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Airlines "American Airlines").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_Hendrickson#cite_note-Gaines16-2)

In 1955, Hendrickson was enrolled at Munster's public elementary school, frequently being praised by her teachers as "a good student and obedient child".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_Hendrickson#cite_note-Gaines17-3) However, she eventually found herself bored with school in Munster, and at age 16 was able to convince her parents to let her stay with her aunt in Florida, where she enrolled at a [Fort Lauderdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Lauderdale,_Florida "Fort Lauderdale, Florida") high school. An adventurous and rebellious teenager, Hendrickson never completed high school, dropping out at the age of 17 in favor of moving from state to state with her boyfriend before settling in Florida, where she was hired by two professional divers who ran an aquarium fish business.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_Hendrickson#cite_note-Gaines23-4) A strong swimmer who had once been on her high school's swim team, Hendrickson quickly learned to dive and began collecting tropical fish off the [Florida Keys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida_Keys "Florida Keys") to sell to [aquarists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquarists "Aquarists") and pet stores.

Aside from her work as a diver, Hendrickson also worked part of the year as a lobster fisherman, and would occasionally take the summer off to volunteer on paleontological digs. She later moved to [Seattle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle "Seattle"), earned her [GED](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Equivalency_Diploma "General Equivalency Diploma"), and considered enrolling at the [University of Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Washington "University of Washington") in order to pursue a [marine biology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_biology "Marine biology") degree, but decided against it, leaving Seattle after a year and moving back to Florida to pursue her diving career.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_Hendrickson#cite_note-Gaines26-5)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sue_Hendrickson&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

In 1970, Hendrickson had a large circle of friends in the diving business, and one day was invited to participate in a [salvage diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wreck_diving "Wreck diving") expedition off the Florida Keys, which she eagerly undertook. Her job was to retrieve valuable building materials that were stored in a cargo freighter which ran aground on a [coral reef](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coral_reef "Coral reef").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_Hendrickson#cite_note-Gaines29-6) While continuing her work in salvage, Hendrickson soon found herself exploring old shipwrecks, later going to the [Dominican Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominican_Republic "Dominican Republic"). She was fascinated by working in the company of archaeologists and fell in love with the country, visiting the island often.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_Hendrickson#cite_note-Gaines35-7)

By the mid-1980s, Hendrickson had also attempted mining [amber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominican_amber "Dominican amber") in the Dominican mountains. She had become one of the largest amber providers for scientists. Hendrickson also found three perfect 23-million-year-old butterflies, which make up a half of the whole world's total collection. Although she found the work too monotonous to pursue full-time, writing that "You could dig for months and find nothing in the Dominican caves,"[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_Hendrickson#cite_note-Gaines37-8) she continued studying [paleo entomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entomology "Entomology"), becoming an expert at identifying fossilized insects.

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fc/Sues_skeleton.jpg/250px-Sues_skeleton.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sues_skeleton.jpg)

[_T. rex_ specimen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur) "Sue (dinosaur)") discovered by Sue Hendrickson

She also met Swiss paleontologist Kirby Siber, who allowed her to join his team consisting of paleontologists Carlos Martin and [Peter Larson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Larson "Peter Larson").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_Hendrickson#cite_note-Gaines41-9) The group began excavating [Miocene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miocene_epoch "Miocene epoch")[baleen whale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baleen_whale "Baleen whale") fossils at an ancient seabed in Peru, and Hendrickson joined the team for several summers, discovering fossilized dolphins, whales, and sharks.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_Hendrickson#cite_note-Gaines41-9) She later accompanied Larson to the [Black Hills Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Hills_Institute "Black Hills Institute") in South Dakota. By this time, paleontology had become her main passion.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_Hendrickson#cite_note-Gaines44-10) On August 12, 1990, while examining a cliff-side in South Dakota with a team from the Black Hills Institute, she discovered a _Tyrannosaurus rex_ specimen – the largest, most complete, and best preserved _T. rex_ ever found. The specimen was later named "[Sue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur) "Sue (dinosaur)")" in her honor.

In 1992, Hendrickson joined a team of marine [archaeologists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology "Archaeology") headed by [Franck Goddio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franck_Goddio "Franck Goddio"). With them, she took part in many diving expeditions, the most notable of which were the Royal Quarters of [Cleopatra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleopatra_VII "Cleopatra VII"), and [Napoleon Bonaparte's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleon_I_of_France "Napoleon I of France") lost fleet from the [Battle of the Nile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Nile "Battle of the Nile").

In 2005, [_Glamour_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glamour_(magazine) "Glamour (magazine)") magazine honored her in their "Glamour Woman of the Year Awards". In 2001, she published an autobiography entitled _Hunt for the Past: My Life as an Explorer_ (New York, NY: Scholastic, Inc). In 2008, she was featured on the "Dare to Explore" chapter of _[National Geographic Kids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National\_Geographic\_Kids "National Geographic Kids")_.

Hendrickson now[_[when?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers#Chronological\_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_] lives on the island of [Guanaja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guanaja "Guanaja"), off the coast of [Honduras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honduras "Honduras"). She is a member of the [Paleontological Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paleontological_Society "Paleontological Society"), [Explorers Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Explorers_Club "The Explorers Club"), [Society for Historical Archaeology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Society_for_Historical_Archaeology "Society for Historical Archaeology"), and was awarded an [honorary Ph.D.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honorary_doctorate "Honorary doctorate") from the [University of Illinois at Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago "University of Illinois at Chicago") in 2000.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_Hendrickson#cite_note-officialsite-11)

The **Black Hills Institute of Geological Research, Inc.** (BHI) is a private [corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporation "Corporation") specializing in the excavation and preparation of [fossils](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fossil "Fossil"), as well as the sale of both original fossil material and museum-quality replicas. Founded in 1974 and based in [Hill City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hill_City,_South_Dakota "Hill City, South Dakota"), [South Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Dakota "South Dakota"), the company is most famous for excavating and selling replicas of some of the most complete [specimens of _Tyrannosaurus rex_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Specimens_of_Tyrannosaurus "Specimens of Tyrannosaurus"), including "[Sue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur) "Sue (dinosaur)")", "[Stan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_(dinosaur) "Stan (dinosaur)")", and "[Trix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trix_(dinosaur) "Trix (dinosaur)")".[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Hills_Institute#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Hills_Institute#cite_note-2)

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/2/23/MuseumHillCitySD.jpg/250px-MuseumHillCitySD.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:MuseumHillCitySD.jpg)

The Black Hills Museum of Natural History

In March 1992, BHI owners founded the **Black Hills Museum of Natural History** in Hill City, a non-profit paleontological museum which is controlled by an independent Board of Directors.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Hills_Institute#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Hills_Institute#cite_note-4)

In May 1992, the remains of "Sue" were seized from the BHI by the [Federal Bureau of Investigation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Bureau_of_Investigation "Federal Bureau of Investigation") and were auctioned off five years later to the [Field Museum of Natural History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_Museum_of_Natural_History "Field Museum of Natural History") in [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago "Chicago"), [Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois "Illinois") for [US$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_dollar "United States dollar")7.6 million– the highest price ever paid for a fossil at the time.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Hills_Institute#cite_note-5)

In 2012, President [Peter Larson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Larson "Peter Larson") fired his brother, Neal, from the Black Hills Institute amid personal differences. Neal, owning a 35% share of the company, filed a lawsuit against Larson and others in 2015 alleging that he was being oppressed as a shareholder. He sought to liquidate the company to buy out his 35% share ownership and part ways. The court ruled that Neal’s shareholder rights had been violated when he was not invited nor allowed to speak at the meeting where he was fired. The Black Hills Institute did not have enough cash for a buyout, causing Larson's fossil collection to be appraised. Several years later, the court ruled that Neal would receive the _Tyrannosaurus rex_ skeleton "Stan", which was appraised at a value of $6 million at the time. "Stan" was sold for $32 million in 2020.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Hills_Institute#cite_note-6)

The **Black Hills Institute of Geological Research, Inc.** (BHI) is a private [corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporation "Corporation") specializing in the excavation and preparation of [fossils](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fossil "Fossil"), as well as the sale of both original fossil material and museum-quality replicas. Founded in 1974 and based in [Hill City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hill_City,_South_Dakota "Hill City, South Dakota"), [South Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Dakota "South Dakota"), the company is most famous for excavating and selling replicas of some of the most complete [specimens of _Tyrannosaurus rex_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Specimens_of_Tyrannosaurus "Specimens of Tyrannosaurus"), including "[Sue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur) "Sue (dinosaur)")", "[Stan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_(dinosaur) "Stan (dinosaur)")", and "[Trix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trix_(dinosaur) "Trix (dinosaur)")".[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Hills_Institute#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Hills_Institute#cite_note-2)

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/2/23/MuseumHillCitySD.jpg/250px-MuseumHillCitySD.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:MuseumHillCitySD.jpg)

The Black Hills Museum of Natural History

In March 1992, BHI owners founded the **Black Hills Museum of Natural History** in Hill City, a non-profit paleontological museum which is controlled by an independent Board of Directors.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Hills_Institute#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Hills_Institute#cite_note-4)

In May 1992, the remains of "Sue" were seized from the BHI by the [Federal Bureau of Investigation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Bureau_of_Investigation "Federal Bureau of Investigation") and were auctioned off five years later to the [Field Museum of Natural History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_Museum_of_Natural_History "Field Museum of Natural History") in [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago "Chicago"), [Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois "Illinois") for [US$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_dollar "United States dollar")7.6 million– the highest price ever paid for a fossil at the time.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Hills_Institute#cite_note-5)

In 2012, President [Peter Larson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Larson "Peter Larson") fired his brother, Neal, from the Black Hills Institute amid personal differences. Neal, owning a 35% share of the company, filed a lawsuit against Larson and others in 2015 alleging that he was being oppressed as a shareholder. He sought to liquidate the company to buy out his 35% share ownership and part ways. The court ruled that Neal’s shareholder rights had been violated when he was not invited nor allowed to speak at the meeting where he was fired. The Black Hills Institute did not have enough cash for a buyout, causing Larson's fossil collection to be appraised. Several years later, the court ruled that Neal would receive the _Tyrannosaurus rex_ skeleton "Stan", which was appraised at a value of $6 million at the time. "Stan" was sold for $32 million in 2020.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Hills_Institute#cite_note-6)

### Mesozoic Vertebrate Life  
 by Darren Tanke and Kenneth Carpenter (eds.)

[Indiana University Press,](http://www.indiana.edu/~iupress/) 2001, 352 pp.  
 0-253-33907-3, $49.95[![Image 1](https://palaeo-electronica.org/2002_1/books/images/meso.jpg)](http://www.indiana.edu/~iupress/books/0-253-33907-3.shtml)

[![Image 2](https://palaeo-electronica.org/2002_1/books/images/john.jpg)](javascript:;)

After 25 years of research on dinosaurs and other aspects of Mesozoic vertebrate life, Royal Tyrrell Museum Paleontologist Phil Currie received quite a surprise late in 2001. His friends honored him by secretly preparing a volume celebrating his considerable contributions to the field. This volume, **Mesozoic Vertebrate Life,** is part of an expanding series of "Life of the Past" paleontology books published by Indiana University Press, conceived and master-edited by Jim Farlow of Indiana University-Purdue University, Fort Wayne. As the book’s acknowledgments note, Phil’s wife Eva Koppelhus was a co-conspirator in bringing this surprise to fruition, along with an impressive array of artists and scientists from around the globe. It’s a touching story and a striking symbol of the respect and many friendships Phil has cultivated so far.

The volume is a collection of papers, from minor notes to descriptions of new species, review articles, philosophical essays, and other analyses, but mostly original research. **Mesozoic Vertebrate Life** is organized into sections on theropod, sauropod, and ornithischian dinosaurs, plus general sections on Mesozoic faunas, paleopathologies, ichnologies, and a final section of two papers on "Dinosaurs and human history." In the middle of the volume, as is common in the "Life of the Past" series, there are 13 pages of full color plates including original and republished artwork by many prominent paleoartisans, plus three lovely sets of color photos of the "feathered dinosaurs" from China.

Appropriately, near the end of the volume there is an extensive and well-structured bibliography of Currie’s books, technical papers, and nontechical publications. The 12 pages of this bibliography demonstrate of the scope of Phil Currie’s work: 16 books as first author or editor, many papers on animals ranging from basal tetrapods to birds, and a lifelong commitment to public education through the popular literature. Not surprisingly, as a technical volume, few papers in **Mesozoic Vertebrate Life** will be of interest to non-specialists, although the final two entries are understandable even to non-scientists. The attractive artwork alone will attract some enthusiasts to cough up the reasonable $50 hardcover price. Because of the diversity of studies in the volume, anyone studying dinosaurs will probably find several papers matching their research interests. There is no unified theme or much cross-referencing connecting the papers, except that almost all of them focus exclusively on extinct dinosaurs.

One obvious omission from the volume is that there is barely a mention of the animals that Currie’s masters and doctoral theses focused on: the synapsid "pelycosaurs" and assorted diapsid reptiles such as **Tangasaurus** and **Youngina** (although Bob Carroll does provide an informative foreword that mentions Phil’s early research on these animals under Bob’s supervision). Additionally, only one paper (Padian et al., with the color plates) discusses the feathered dinosaurs that have captured Phil’s attention so prominently in recent years.

The papers vary widely in length, technical level, and overall scientific quality as well as subject matter. Consequently I cannot offer detailed commentary on each of them, but I will discuss some that will draw the most attention from readers. Dan Chure offers a succinct and convincing argument that AMNH 5780, widely considered to be the only existing type material for **Laelaps trihedrodon** Cope 1877, is indistinguishable from **Allosaurus**teeth and is not part of the type material, so Cope’s species rests on shaky taxonomic ground. Hans Larsson provides a detailed description of a brain endocast of **Carcharodontosaurus**, and incorporates this into a larger dataset to show how the brain evolved on the line to crown group birds. The brain anatomy and dimensions of **Carcharodontosaurus** seem grossly similar to crocodylians, unlike the more derived brains of coelurosaurian dinosaurs, including birds. Likewise, Peter Makovicky describes similar features in a braincase of **Montanaceratops**. Phil Currie’s research has frequently delved into the intricacies of skull anatomy in dinosaurs, so these are fitting entries to the volume.

Other entries interpret dinosaur fossil anatomy and function, with varying degrees of rigor. Carpenter and Smith present their long-awaited analysis of the forelimb anatomy of **Tyrannosaurus rex.** Their description and illustrations of osteological features are useful, but they have rather uncritically used avian muscle anatomy to reconstruct **Tyrannosaurus** myology, eschewing methodological approaches such as Witmer’s extant phylogenetic bracket. As such, the significance of their biomechanical analysis will remain controversial. Yet their reconstruction was barely used for the biomechanical analysis anyway, and the analysis itself says little other than that **Tyrannosaurus** had some freedom of joint motion allowing its forelimbs to exert forces of questionable magnitude and utility relative to its size.

Padian et al. describe previously unrecognized skeletal and integumentary features of the Chinese "feathered dinosaurs." Their analysis refutes two controversial hypotheses, that feathers evolved for flight and that the fibers on **Sinosauropteryx** (and other coelurosaur) specimens are merely collagenous or non-integumentary structures. They consider other uses of early feathers such as insulation, and infer how these feathers and various skeletal elements contributed to the evolution of flight.

Farlow uses morphometrics on theropod foot skeletons and tracks to show that it is unreasonable to assign trackmakers to taxa based on size alone. He argues, however, that other lines of evidence such as track vs. body fossil correspondences in space and time can be useful. Farlow applies this approach to Comanchean footprints of large theropods and asserts that **Acrocanthosaurus** is the "most likely maker" of these tracks, having a wide home range that might have spanned many types of habitats and ichnofacies.

Descriptive reviews and compilations of data from ornithomimosaur jaws (Hurum), Montanan oviraptorosaurs (Varrichio), tyrannosaurid systematics (Holtz), juvenile hadrosaurs from Dinosaur Provincial Park (Tanke and Brett-Surman), Albertan, Two Medicine, and North American dinosaur faunas (Ryan and Russell; Trexler; Lehman), pathologies of theropod bones (Rothschild et al.; Molnar) and amniote eggshells (Hirsch), and quadrupedal ornithopod trackways (Lockley and Wright) are all useful resources for specialists interested in these particular subjects. The final chapter by Sarjeant is an entertaining history of the portrayal of dinosaurs in popular fiction since their discovery. He points out that dinosaurs did not become huge media stars until recently, especially in the 1970s, and that like science fiction and actual technology, dinosaur fiction sometimes corresponded to future scientific ideas about dinosaur biology.

As usual in a festschrift volume, some new species are dedicated to Phil Currie. Skeletal elements from a new basal theropod (**Quilmesaurus**… named after Quilmes, Currie’s favorite cerveza?) and a new bird trackway (**Aquatilavipes**, coined by Currie in 1981) each receive the species (or ichnospecies) name **curriei** in honor of Phil’s work on these subjects.

All things considered, this volume is not an urgent purchase for dinosaur specialists, but it should become a part of their library. Considering the fair price and production quality, there is no need to wait for a paperback version. Paleontologists, hobbyists, and others working outside of the clade Dinosauria have no strong reason to buy it. Find a copy of it and read the Carroll foreword and the bibliography to learn more about Phil Currie, or scan the artwork and read the Sarjeant entry for some dinosaurian fun.

This volume provides some tantalizing, but not shocking or revolutionary, glimpses into the life of the Mesozoic, a life that we’d all love to know better.As for Phil Currie, if you’ve met him you want to get to know him well too. This book honors him by showing how he has inspired a generation of scientists and artists. A volume in 2026 celebrating Phil’s work over the next 25 years will be truly stunning. Then perhaps we’ll be the ones who are surprised, by how much he means to vertebrate paleontology.

read/failed entries as observations, not available actions. A failed fetch does not
erase its title, author or snippet. If an identified document is inaccessible and
this batch offers no alternate copy, return that lead for the planner to pursue;
do not replace it with unrelated background reading. Snippets are not full-page evidence.

After reading, open another supplied page only for a remaining identifying relation
or a competing candidate. Return when the local task is established, contradicted,
or has no useful route here; do not keep browsing because the entire question is
unfinished. Page-internal links belong to the recursive reader, not new roots.
Finish normally with a brief candidate update: source-supported relations, conflicts

Depends on the dinosaur.

Some we only have a handful of bones for them, so most of their reconstruction is based on what their near relatives looked like, sorta like reconstructing a tiger when all you have is a fore limb and a house cat to use as a model. You can do pretty good…but if you later find a full tiger skeleton you'll see flaws in your reconstruction. And cats are all pretty similar, species-wise.

Other dinosaurs, the remains are pretty complete, so the reconstructions are naturally going to be better. Still, there is a level of guesswork involved even here, because the fleshy bits that were on those bones can often throw up surprises (though fewer than you'd think).

But then we have a couple where we have actual fossilized mummies of the dinosaurs.

Yes, it could. And this simple fact leads to a much more difficult question: if the emergence of humanity was not guaranteed by evolution, what does that tell us about the presumed purpose of nature — and, more broadly, of the Universe itself?

Life arose on Earth at least 3.5 billion years ago. Roughly 539 million years ago, the Cambrian Explosion began — a period of rapid increase, by geological standards, in animal diversity. Since then, the history of life on Earth has passed through five major mass extinctions and many other catastrophes.

Evolution did not follow a predetermined route toward humanity. Its history was shaped by natural selection, mutations, genetic drift, environmental change, and global catastrophes. Had some events unfolded differently, Homo sapiens might never have appeared.

Imagine an even more radical scenario: what if life on Earth had vanished completely during one of the global catastrophes? Today our planet would be lifeless, and billions of years of terrestrial evolution would have ended without leaving anyone here capable of discovering and understanding that history.

The Emergence of Humanity Was Not Guaranteed

In the history of Earth as we know it, no mechanism has been found that would have guaranteed the preservation of life for the sake of the future emergence of humanity, or of intelligence more generally.

A single mass extinction 66 million years ago radically changed the subsequent history of life. The disappearance of non-avian dinosaurs opened new ecological opportunities for mammals, and tens of millions of years later, humans emerged within one of the evolutionary lineages of mammals.

Change a few links in this chain, and the outcome could have been entirely different.

This is known as historical contingency: evolutionary outcomes depend not only on general laws of nature, but also on the specific sequence of events, which could have unfolded differently.

Humanity is therefore not the obvious endpoint of evolution, but one result of an extraordinarily long history. In this sense, our existence can be called a remarkable stroke of luck — not because we know the exact probability of humanity’s emergence, but because it was never guaranteed.

Does the Universe Have a Purpose?

The contingency of humanity does not prove that the Universe is purposeless. Science has no way to directly establish whether reality as a whole has an ultimate purpose.

But Earth’s history supports a more cautious conclusion: we do not have sufficient grounds to regard the emergence of humanity itself as a predetermined and guaranteed purpose of nature.

If the Universe were intended specifically to produce Homo sapiens, the history of life on Earth looks like a rather unusual way of achieving that purpose: billions of years of evolution, mass extinctions, and a long sequence of events, any one of which could have altered the path that followed.

Moreover, Earth is one planet orbiting one star among an immense number of stars and galaxies. This does not prove that humanity has no special purpose, but neither does it give us grounds to regard ourselves as the center of the Universe.

We should therefore distinguish between two entirely different questions:

Does fundamental reality have any purpose?

and

Is humanity that purpose?

Even an affirmative answer to the first does not imply an affirmative answer to the second.

Fine-Tuning and a Broader Reality

An obvious objection arises: some fundamental parameters of our Universe lie within ranges compatible with the existence of complex structures and life. Could what is known as fine-tuning point to some kind of purpose?

There is no definitive answer yet. Explanations under discussion include deeper physical laws, the anthropic principle and observational selection effects, the Multiverse hypothesis, some form of design, and possibilities still unknown to us.

If our Universe is one of many, observers would naturally find themselves in worlds where conditions allow their existence. But the Multiverse, too, is not yet an established fact.

So the question remains open.

And even if fine-tuning is one day shown to result from some form of design, it still would not follow that Earth and humanity are its central purpose. Any such design might concern the emergence of complexity, life, or intelligence in general — or something entirely unknown to us.

Chance and the Possibility of Intelligent Matter

The statement that “humans appeared by chance” also requires clarification.

Our emergence occurred within a world governed by physical, chemical, and biological laws. Earth’s particular history could have unfolded differently, but reality itself allowed for the possibility of beings like us emerging.

We should therefore distinguish between possibility and its realization.

Humans were not a guaranteed outcome of evolution, but the fundamental properties of our world make the emergence of intelligent matter possible.

And here an even deeper question arises:

why does reality allow the existence of matter capable of organizing itself into cells, organisms, consciousness, and intelligence at all?

We know that this possibility exists because we ourselves are one realization of it. But why fundamental reality has precisely these properties remains an open question.

Perhaps they follow from deeper laws, are in some sense necessary, are explained by a broader reality such as the Multiverse, or by some form of design.

There is also the philosophical possibility that no further explanation exists at all: fundamental reality and its basic properties may simply exist as ultimate facts. In philosophy, such facts are called brute facts.

It is therefore important to distinguish between “we do not know the cause” and “there is no cause”: these are not the same thing.

Perhaps one of the deepest mysteries lies not only in why humanity appeared on Earth, but also in why reality contains the possibility of intelligent matter arising at all.

The Intelligence That Began to Understand the World

There is another astonishing turn in this story.

The cognitive capacities of our ancestors evolved under the pressures of survival and adaptation to Earth’s environment. Yet the intelligence that emerged went far beyond those original tasks.

A brain shaped for life on Earth began to investigate atoms, the origin of species, distant galaxies, space, time, and the history of the Universe.

Evolution did not need to “understand” the Universe in order to produce a being that tries to understand the Universe.

At least on our planet, part of matter acquired the ability to investigate matter, and part of nature acquired the ability to understand nature.

Life on Earth could have existed for billions of years and vanished without ever giving rise here to a being capable of understanding that it had existed at all.

Human intelligence changed that.

If There Is No Ready-Made Purpose

Natural processes in themselves display no moral attitude toward their consequences. An asteroid that destroys species is not evil, and a star that creates conditions for life is not good. In this sense, observable physical nature is morally neutral.

But with the emergence of sentient and intelligent beings come suffering and well-being, and with the development of intelligence and culture come ideas of good and evil, justice, responsibility, and the value of life.

The same is true of purposes.

If humanity was not a predetermined purpose of evolution, it does not follow that human existence is meaningless.

The contingency of our origin does not imply the meaninglessness of our existence.

With the emergence of intelligence came the ability to understand what is happening, choose among alternatives, create values, and consciously set goals.

And here arises one of the most interesting paradoxes of our origin:

we may not have been the purpose of the process that produced us, yet we became beings capable of setting goals of our own.

From Luck to Responsibility

If nature did not guarantee the emergence of human intelligence and does not guarantee its continued existence, then the preservation and further development of humanity become tasks for humanity itself.

We are already capable of detecting asteroids, studying global threats, combating disease, preserving knowledge, and potentially spreading terrestrial life beyond a single planet. What once depended entirely on natural circumstances is gradually also becoming a matter of conscious choice.

We might never have appeared, and we may one day disappear. Our existence can therefore be viewed not as something guaranteed by the structure of the Universe, but as an extraordinarily valuable possibility that has become reality.

Even if some purpose or design lies behind the fundamental structure of reality, we still lack sufficient grounds to regard Earth and humanity as its center.

But regardless of the final answer to the question of purpose, one astonishing fact remains: reality has proved capable of producing matter that lives, feels, thinks, and tries to understand reality itself.

Perhaps intelligence was not a predetermined purpose of nature. But with its emergence came beings capable of understanding reality, creating values, and setting goals for themselves.

And if the Universe did not give us a ready-made purpose, that still does not mean there is no meaning. Perhaps one of the most important features of intelligence is precisely its ability to create a meaningful future where nature provided no ready-made script.

We may not have been the purpose of the Universe. But now we ourselves are capable of setting goals — and we will increasingly shape whatever part of the Universe's future comes within the reach of human intelligence.

![Image 5](https://qph.cf2.quoracdn.net/main-qimg-55cfed6c28166eb82c148036e7039f62)

The main thing that has changed since then, other than just the sheer number of fossils we’ve found, is our technology for examining them in microscopic details. This has allowed us to determine things like muscle attachment points, which mean we’re no longer guessing quite as much about the placement of muscles around the skeleton. Computer simulations allow us to experiment with these models and determine which ones are more plausible. We’ve also been able to find imprints of skin, even in some cases pigments and most famously feathers.

Of course we’ll never absolutely know for certain, but we’re almost definitely closer to a true picture than we ever have been.

When Victorian scientists found a fossilized thumb spike, they mistakenly glued it to an Iguanodon’s nose. Today, reconstructing a dinosaur from its bones is a highly accurate science.

While early museums mounted Tyrannosaurus rex skeletons standing upright, dragging their tails on the ground like scaly kangaroos, modern paleontology relies on biomechanics and comparative anatomy rather than imagination. The process starts with the bones themselves. Modern paleontologists do not just look at the shape of a skeleton; they look for muscle scars. Bones bear deep ridges and anchor points where muscles attached. By mapping these scars and comparing them to the "Extant Phylogenetic Bracket" (a dinosaur's closest living relatives: birds and crocodilians), scientists can accurately reconstruct the size, shape, and layout of the muscle tissue. This biomechanical approach is how researchers learned that T. rex held its spine horizontal to the ground, with a stiffened tail acting as a counterbalance for its massive head.

For a long time, the biggest accuracy problem was not the skeleton, but the "shrink-wrapping" of soft tissue. Paleoartists used to draw skin tightly over the bones, outlining every skull hole and rib. If a modern hippo or swan were shrink-wrapped based solely on their skulls, they would look like terrifying, alien monsters. Dinosaurs likely had much more soft tissue—fat stores, fleshy gums, wattles, and lips covering their teeth.

Recently, technology has allowed paleontology to see beyond the skeleton entirely. Fossilized melanosomes (pigment cells) have been preserved well enough to reveal the actual colors of some dinosaurs, such as the ginger-and-white striped tail of Sinosauropteryx or the iridescent black feathers of Microraptor.

Sometimes, the fossil record skips the reconstruction phase entirely. In 2011, miners in Canada uncovered Borealopelta, a 110-million-year-old heavily armored nodosaur. It was not just a skeleton, but an intact, 3D mummified dinosaur. Preserved rapidly in an undersea landslide, its keratinized scales, defensive spikes, and even its stomach contents were perfectly fossilized. Looking at Borealopelta is not looking at an artist’s guess—it is looking directly at the true face of an armored dinosaur exactly as it appeared in life.

Pretty good, these days.

Of course there's are always exceptions and corrections happen frequently in these cases. Spinosaurus is notoriously controversial, so mich so that many edutainment channels in the paleo space on YouTube refuse to cover it, because whatever they say will likely be wrong in a few years.

Part of the problem is missing bones. Many species are known fron a handful of specimens which, while diagnostic (meaning that they're enough to say, with reasonable certainty, what family of dinosaurs they belong to and that they're not from another, already known species), are far from the complete skeleton. For example, Therezinasaurus has *never* had an intact skull found. We have the rest of the body and some scattered teeth, but no cranium or mandible. Any “paleoaccurate” depiction you see in media, therefore, has a skull extrapolated based on related dinosaurs we DO have skulls for, like Nothrunychus.

The second is non-fossilizing structures. The keratin sheaths on horns, for example, can have shapes wildly different from their boney core.

The third is non-skeletal structures that CAN fossilize, but need the right conditions to do so. Over the past 20 years there have been amazing fossils coming out of China, and new advances in radiometric and computer imaging have shown feathers, quills, and even fossil skin pigment traces, including in fossils that were discovered decades ago. We now have reasonable approximation of coloring for at least two species, and a growing catalogue of dinosaurs we know for certain what their skin looked like.

How accurate is the reconstruction of dinosaurs from skeletons?

We have very few fossil remains for most species of dinosaurs. Having an entire jaw with teeth is much better than average. At that point we say “It looks related to dinosaur species X, for which we have good complete fossils.” and try to guess at the differences. In other words, not very accurate.

For the dinosaurs where we have complete or nearly complete fossils, the skeletal reconstruction is generally quite good (or so we think). That often doesn’t tell you what they looked like. For instance, the skeleton of a yellow bittern suggests this (photo of actual yellow bittern):

We’ve come a long way from the statues of dinosaurs at Crystal Palace Park in London. It was first thought, for example, that Iguanodon was very lizard-like and had a horn on its nose. We now know that it stood upright, the “horn” was actually a thumb-spike, and it probably walked on all-fours, only running bipedally when they want to move fast, probably to avoid being eaten by a predator. In the intervening years, a lot more skeletons have been uncovered, and as our understanding of dinosaur anatomy improves, skeletal reconstructions have been increasingly accurate. The most familiar type of fossils are permineralized bones. Bones are composed of a mineral (hydroxyapatite) and a protein (collagen). When an animal dies and the body is deposited in mineral-rich water, as the organic collagen decomposes, minerals from the water can attach to the hydroxyapatite, replacing the organic material. The minerals don't decompose, so the skeleton ends up “turning to stone” at the cellular level.

If the remains are buried under additional sediment, they are protected from the forces of erosion until they are eventually recovered.

Contrary to popular belief, permineralization can happen relatively quickly-a few years or decades is often enough to completely mineralize a bone, if the conditions are suitable. The mineralized bones can then last for millions of years, relatively unchanged.

[Permineralization - Wikipedia](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permineralization "en.m.wikipedia.org")

There are other ways that organisms can be preserved as fossils (freezing, mummification, deposition in anaerobic conditions, etc.), but Permineralization is the most common.

Hope that helps.

In a period of doubt in my life I collected road kill and other such finds and extracted the bones.

I scrambled them up (each animal’s by itself) and found that there was always a clear best match when mating bones of a mature animal (the still born foal lost the ends of its major limb bones while being buried for a few years). I did that as a novice, albeit an engineer of scientific equipment. After that and a horse I got to where I could pick up a fragment of bone out in the boonies and tell you which part of which limb it was, which vertebra within a position or two or three.

I find the claims of paleontologists to the validity of their reconstructions from partial skeletons to be readily believable.

Depends on the dinosaur.

Some we only have a handful of bones for them, so most of their reconstruction is based on what their near relatives looked like, sorta like reconstructing a tiger when all you have is a fore limb and a house cat to use as a model. You can do pretty good…but if you later find a full tiger skeleton you'll see flaws in your reconstruction. And cats are all pretty similar, species-wise.

Other dinosaurs, the remains are pretty complete, so the reconstructions are naturally going to be better. Still, there is a level of guesswork involved even here, because the fleshy bits that were on those bones can often throw up surprises (though fewer than you'd think).

But then we have a couple where we have actual fossilized mummies of the dinosaurs.

Yes, it could. And this simple fact leads to a much more difficult question: if the emergence of humanity was not guaranteed by evolution, what does that tell us about the presumed purpose of nature — and, more broadly, of the Universe itself?

Life arose on Earth at least 3.5 billion years ago. Roughly 539 million years ago, the Cambrian Explosion began — a period of rapid increase, by geological standards, in animal diversity. Since then, the history of life on Earth has passed through five major mass extinctions and many other catastrophes.

Evolution did not follow a predetermined route toward humanity. Its history was shaped by natural selection, mutations, genetic drift, environmental change, and global catastrophes. Had some events unfolded differently, Homo sapiens might never have appeared.

Imagine an even more radical scenario: what if life on Earth had vanished completely during one of the global catastrophes? Today our planet would be lifeless, and billions of years of terrestrial evolution would have ended without leaving anyone here capable of discovering and understanding that history.

The Emergence of Humanity Was Not Guaranteed

In the history of Earth as we know it, no mechanism has been found that would have guaranteed the preservation of life for the sake of the future emergence of humanity, or of intelligence more generally.

A single mass extinction 66 million years ago radically changed the subsequent history of life. The disappearance of non-avian dinosaurs opened new ecological opportunities for mammals, and tens of millions of years later, humans emerged within one of the evolutionary lineages of mammals.

Change a few links in this chain, and the outcome could have been entirely different.

This is known as historical contingency: evolutionary outcomes depend not only on general laws of nature, but also on the specific sequence of events, which could have unfolded differently.

Humanity is therefore not the obvious endpoint of evolution, but one result of an extraordinarily long history. In this sense, our existence can be called a remarkable stroke of luck — not because we know the exact probability of humanity’s emergence, but because it was never guaranteed.

Does the Universe Have a Purpose?

The contingency of humanity does not prove that the Universe is purposeless. Science has no way to directly establish whether reality as a whole has an ultimate purpose.

But Earth’s history supports a more cautious conclusion: we do not have sufficient grounds to regard the emergence of humanity itself as a predetermined and guaranteed purpose of nature.

If the Universe were intended specifically to produce Homo sapiens, the history of life on Earth looks like a rather unusual way of achieving that purpose: billions of years of evolution, mass extinctions, and a long sequence of events, any one of which could have altered the path that followed.

Moreover, Earth is one planet orbiting one star among an immense number of stars and galaxies. This does not prove that humanity has no special purpose, but neither does it give us grounds to regard ourselves as the center of the Universe.

We should therefore distinguish between two entirely different questions:

Does fundamental reality have any purpose?

and

Is humanity that purpose?

Even an affirmative answer to the first does not imply an affirmative answer to the second.

Fine-Tuning and a Broader Reality

An obvious objection arises: some fundamental parameters of our Universe lie within ranges compatible with the existence of complex structures and life. Could what is known as fine-tuning point to some kind of purpose?

There is no definitive answer yet. Explanations under discussion include deeper physical laws, the anthropic principle and observational selection effects, the Multiverse hypothesis, some form of design, and possibilities still unknown to us.

If our Universe is one of many, observers would naturally find themselves in worlds where conditions allow their existence. But the Multiverse, too, is not yet an established fact.

So the question remains open.

And even if fine-tuning is one day shown to result from some form of design, it still would not follow that Earth and humanity are its central purpose. Any such design might concern the emergence of complexity, life, or intelligence in general — or something entirely unknown to us.

Chance and the Possibility of Intelligent Matter

The statement that “humans appeared by chance” also requires clarification.

Our emergence occurred within a world governed by physical, chemical, and biological laws. Earth’s particular history could have unfolded differently, but reality itself allowed for the possibility of beings like us emerging.

We should therefore distinguish between possibility and its realization.

Humans were not a guaranteed outcome of evolution, but the fundamental properties of our world make the emergence of intelligent matter possible.

And here an even deeper question arises:

why does reality allow the existence of matter capable of organizing itself into cells, organisms, consciousness, and intelligence at all?

We know that this possibility exists because we ourselves are one realization of it. But why fundamental reality has precisely these properties remains an open question.

Perhaps they follow from deeper laws, are in some sense necessary, are explained by a broader reality such as the Multiverse, or by some form of design.

There is also the philosophical possibility that no further explanation exists at all: fundamental reality and its basic properties may simply exist as ultimate facts. In philosophy, such facts are called brute facts.

It is therefore important to distinguish between “we do not know the cause” and “there is no cause”: these are not the same thing.

Perhaps one of the deepest mysteries lies not only in why humanity appeared on Earth, but also in why reality contains the possibility of intelligent matter arising at all.

The Intelligence That Began to Understand the World

There is another astonishing turn in this story.

The cognitive capacities of our ancestors evolved under the pressures of survival and adaptation to Earth’s environment. Yet the intelligence that emerged went far beyond those original tasks.

A brain shaped for life on Earth began to investigate atoms, the origin of species, distant galaxies, space, time, and the history of the Universe.

Evolution did not need to “understand” the Universe in order to produce a being that tries to understand the Universe.

At least on our planet, part of matter acquired the ability to investigate matter, and part of nature acquired the ability to understand nature.

Life on Earth could have existed for billions of years and vanished without ever giving rise here to a being capable of understanding that it had existed at all.

Human intelligence changed that.

If There Is No Ready-Made Purpose

Natural processes in themselves display no moral attitude toward their consequences. An asteroid that destroys species is not evil, and a star that creates conditions for life is not good. In this sense, observable physical nature is morally neutral.

But with the emergence of sentient and intelligent beings come suffering and well-being, and with the development of intelligence and culture come ideas of good and evil, justice, responsibility, and the value of life.

The same is true of purposes.

If humanity was not a predetermined purpose of evolution, it does not follow that human existence is meaningless.

The contingency of our origin does not imply the meaninglessness of our existence.

With the emergence of intelligence came the ability to understand what is happening, choose among alternatives, create values, and consciously set goals.

And here arises one of the most interesting paradoxes of our origin:

we may not have been the purpose of the process that produced us, yet we became beings capable of setting goals of our own.

From Luck to Responsibility

If nature did not guarantee the emergence of human intelligence and does not guarantee its continued existence, then the preservation and further development of humanity become tasks for humanity itself.

We are already capable of detecting asteroids, studying global threats, combating disease, preserving knowledge, and potentially spreading terrestrial life beyond a single planet. What once depended entirely on natural circumstances is gradually also becoming a matter of conscious choice.

We might never have appeared, and we may one day disappear. Our existence can therefore be viewed not as something guaranteed by the structure of the Universe, but as an extraordinarily valuable possibility that has become reality.

Even if some purpose or design lies behind the fundamental structure of reality, we still lack sufficient grounds to regard Earth and humanity as its center.

But regardless of the final answer to the question of purpose, one astonishing fact remains: reality has proved capable of producing matter that lives, feels, thinks, and tries to understand reality itself.

Perhaps intelligence was not a predetermined purpose of nature. But with its emergence came beings capable of understanding reality, creating values, and setting goals for themselves.

And if the Universe did not give us a ready-made purpose, that still does not mean there is no meaning. Perhaps one of the most important features of intelligence is precisely its ability to create a meaningful future where nature provided no ready-made script.

We may not have been the purpose of the Universe. But now we ourselves are capable of setting goals — and we will increasingly shape whatever part of the Universe's future comes within the reach of human intelligence.

The main thing that has changed since then, other than just the sheer number of fossils we’ve found, is our technology for examining them in microscopic details. This has allowed us to determine things like muscle attachment points, which mean we’re no longer guessing quite as much about the placement of muscles around the skeleton. Computer simulations allow us to experiment with these models and determine which ones are more plausible. We’ve also been able to find imprints of skin, even in some cases pigments and most famously feathers.

Of course we’ll never absolutely know for certain, but we’re almost definitely closer to a true picture than we ever have been.

When Victorian scientists found a fossilized thumb spike, they mistakenly glued it to an Iguanodon’s nose. Today, reconstructing a dinosaur from its bones is a highly accurate science.

While early museums mounted Tyrannosaurus rex skeletons standing upright, dragging their tails on the ground like scaly kangaroos, modern paleontology relies on biomechanics and comparative anatomy rather than imagination. The process starts with the bones themselves. Modern paleontologists do not just look at the shape of a skeleton; they look for muscle scars. Bones bear deep ridges and anchor points where muscles attached. By mapping these scars and comparing them to the "Extant Phylogenetic Bracket" (a dinosaur's closest living relatives: birds and crocodilians), scientists can accurately reconstruct the size, shape, and layout of the muscle tissue. This biomechanical approach is how researchers learned that T. rex held its spine horizontal to the ground, with a stiffened tail acting as a counterbalance for its massive head.

For a long time, the biggest accuracy problem was not the skeleton, but the "shrink-wrapping" of soft tissue. Paleoartists used to draw skin tightly over the bones, outlining every skull hole and rib. If a modern hippo or swan were shrink-wrapped based solely on their skulls, they would look like terrifying, alien monsters. Dinosaurs likely had much more soft tissue—fat stores, fleshy gums, wattles, and lips covering their teeth.

Recently, technology has allowed paleontology to see beyond the skeleton entirely. Fossilized melanosomes (pigment cells) have been preserved well enough to reveal the actual colors of some dinosaurs, such as the ginger-and-white striped tail of Sinosauropteryx or the iridescent black feathers of Microraptor.

Sometimes, the fossil record skips the reconstruction phase entirely. In 2011, miners in Canada uncovered Borealopelta, a 110-million-year-old heavily armored nodosaur. It was not just a skeleton, but an intact, 3D mummified dinosaur. Preserved rapidly in an undersea landslide, its keratinized scales, defensive spikes, and even its stomach contents were perfectly fossilized. Looking at Borealopelta is not looking at an artist’s guess—it is looking directly at the true face of an armored dinosaur exactly as it appeared in life.

Pretty good, these days.

Of course there's are always exceptions and corrections happen frequently in these cases. Spinosaurus is notoriously controversial, so mich so that many edutainment channels in the paleo space on YouTube refuse to cover it, because whatever they say will likely be wrong in a few years.

Part of the problem is missing bones. Many species are known fron a handful of specimens which, while diagnostic (meaning that they're enough to say, with reasonable certainty, what family of dinosaurs they belong to and that they're not from another, already known species), are far from the complete skeleton. For example, Therezinasaurus has *never* had an intact skull found. We have the rest of the body and some scattered teeth, but no cranium or mandible. Any “paleoaccurate” depiction you see in media, therefore, has a skull extrapolated based on related dinosaurs we DO have skulls for, like Nothrunychus.

The second is non-fossilizing structures. The keratin sheaths on horns, for example, can have shapes wildly different from their boney core.

The third is non-skeletal structures that CAN fossilize, but need the right conditions to do so. Over the past 20 years there have been amazing fossils coming out of China, and new advances in radiometric and computer imaging have shown feathers, quills, and even fossil skin pigment traces, including in fossils that were discovered decades ago. We now have reasonable approximation of coloring for at least two species, and a growing catalogue of dinosaurs we know for certain what their skin looked like.

How accurate is the reconstruction of dinosaurs from skeletons?

We have very few fossil remains for most species of dinosaurs. Having an entire jaw with teeth is much better than average. At that point we say “It looks related to dinosaur species X, for which we have good complete fossils.” and try to guess at the differences. In other words, not very accurate.

For the dinosaurs where we have complete or nearly complete fossils, the skeletal reconstruction is generally quite good (or so we think). That often doesn’t tell you what they looked like. For instance, the skeleton of a yellow bittern suggests this (photo of actual yellow bittern):

The most familiar type of fossils are permineralized bones. Bones are composed of a mineral (hydroxyapatite) and a protein (collagen). When an animal dies and the body is deposited in mineral-rich water, as the organic collagen decomposes, minerals from the water can attach to the hydroxyapatite, replacing the organic material. The minerals don't decompose, so the skeleton ends up “turning to stone” at the cellular level.

If the remains are buried under additional sediment, they are protected from the forces of erosion until they are eventually recovered.

Contrary to popular belief, permineralization can happen relatively quickly-a few years or decades is often enough to completely mineralize a bone, if the conditions are suitable. The mineralized bones can then last for millions of years, relatively unchanged.

[Permineralization - Wikipedia](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permineralization "en.m.wikipedia.org")

There are other ways that organisms can be preserved as fossils (freezing, mummification, deposition in anaerobic conditions, etc.), but Permineralization is the most common.

Hope that helps.

In a period of doubt in my life I collected road kill and other such finds and extracted the bones.

I scrambled them up (each animal’s by itself) and found that there was always a clear best match when mating bones of a mature animal (the still born foal lost the ends of its major limb bones while being buried for a few years). I was able to find a best pairing of every bone in the hands and feet of a cat, a dog, and a racoon.

I did that as a novice, albeit an engineer of scientific equipment. After that and a horse I got to where I could pick up a fragment of bone out in the boonies and tell you which part of which limb it was, which vertebra within a position or two or three.

I find the claims of paleontologists to the validity of their reconstructions from partial skeletons to be readily believable.

Read pages for a research assistant and follow useful links recursively. During
extraction, only the supplied page is evidence. The question defines what to look
for; parent reasoning guides navigation but is not this page's evidence.
Extraction uses the original question and current page, not the search query or
parent's hypothesis. Keep facts relevant to any part of the original question.
During navigation, a supplied local relation is a task, not evidence. Follow links
that establish or contradict it. Return when it is settled or has no useful route
here; other unresolved relations belong to the parent. Do not solve the whole
question again inside every branch.

Preserve exact relevant names and rows with their headers, values, units, dates
and scope. Never replace relevant rows with ellipses, examples or instructions to
continue the list. If all rows cannot fit, prioritize rows useful to the question
and explicitly mark omissions. A partial, restricted or truncated list is not the
complete candidate set. Missing fields are unknown. Keep relevant discoveries even
if they answer a different part of the original question.

Follow links likely to fill a candidate's missing condition or reach the required
document/year. An index is useful when it offers a concrete route to the needed
record; generic menus or keyword collections alone do not justify expansion.
Link-menu rank is only a hint: check the destination's subject and scope. If content
repeats, try a detail page or another supported route. Links outside the menu and inferred
paths on an observed site are allowed. Child notes are returned automatically;
do not copy their facts into your own note. Retain useful unvisited links even
when expansion stops.

For extraction return:
**Final Information**
**Page:** Actual title and URL.
**Evidence:** Exact relevant facts/rows and short supporting quotes.
**Connections:** Candidate and identifying relation supported or contradicted here; label deductions.
**Coverage:** Actual entities, years, population; full list, subset or excerpt.
**Missing:** Requested fields this page does not establish.
**Next links:** One URL and missing relation per line, most useful first. With Expand yes,
the first eligible route is executed without another selection call, within the budget.
**Expand:** yes or no, and why.
**Status:** partial
Use answered only if this page supplies all requested facts, partial for useful
incomplete evidence, or not_found with a brief reason. During navigation, call
web_fetch or reply DONE.

# Fossilized Footprints

![Image 6: Artistic impression of ice age animals gathered around Lake Otero.](https://www.nps.gov/whsa/learn/nature/images/Trackways.jpg?maxwidth=1300&maxheight=1300&autorotate=false&format=webp)

Scientists are studying fossil footprints at White Sands to better understand the Ice Age ecosystem of Lake Otero. 
NPS Photo

![Image 7: Human fossilized footprint in gypsum soil.](https://www.nps.gov/whsa/learn/nature/images/Human-fossilized-footprints-at-White-Sands-National-Park.jpg?maxwidth=650&autorotate=false)

White Sands has the largest collection of fossilized human footprints. 
NPS Photo

Every day, people from all over the world visit White Sands National Park and leave traces of their adventures. The white dunes of the Tularosa Basin are just a recent occurrence on the geological timeline. At White Sands, we find many remarkable fossilized footprints scattered across Lake Otero. While these footprints are ancient, scientists are still uncovering new evidence of past life.   
  
 Tens of thousands of years ago, during the ice age, a giant body of water, Lake Otero, rested within the Tularosa basin. The climate was less arid, and the vegetation was abundant. One could have seen grasslands stretching for miles that would have looked more like the prairies of the Midwest rather than New Mexico’s deserts.  
  
 This paradise of lush green life naturally captured the attention of the larger animals of the ice age. Plant eaters such as ancient camels, Columbian mammoths and Harlan’s ground sloth came to Lake Otero to feast on the grasses and trees of the Tularosa Basin. This attracted fearsome predators known as the dire wolf and American Lion. These animals’ footprints remained long after their departure of the wetlands of Lake Otero and eventually became fossilized.  
  
 The latest research shows that humans have been living in North America and Tularosa Basin for at least 23,000 years. It was previously thought that humans arrived in North America closer to 13,500 – 16,000 years ago.   
  
 Research was conducted to see what could be found below the surface by digging a trench in the gypsum soil on the park’s western playa. Human Footprints were found within different layers of sediment below the surface of the dig site. Above and below these footprints were ancient grass seeds (_Ruppia cirrhosa_) which were analyzed using radiocarbon dating. It was revealed that the calibrated dates were of 22,860 (∓320) and 21,130 (∓250) years ago.

![Image 8: Teenagers walking and standing on the shore of a wetlands in a muddy, grassy environment making footprints in the mud.](https://www.nps.gov/whsa/learn/nature/images/Teenagers-left-their-footprints-in-the-mud_1.jpg?maxwidth=1300&maxheight=1300&autorotate=false&format=webp)

Do the important things in life change? Long before the sand dunes formed at White Sands National Park, teenagers left their footprints in the mud, only to be discovered thousands of years later to reveal what daily life may have been like during the ice age. 
© Davide Bonadonna and Bournemouth University

![Image 9: A trench dug into the brown gypsum soil on a lake playa in White Sands National Park.](https://www.nps.gov/whsa/learn/nature/images/Trench-dug-into-gypsum-soil-at-White-Sands-revealing-more-human-footprints_1.jpg?maxwidth=650&autorotate=false)

A trench dug into the brown gypsum soil on a lake playa in White Sands National Park reveals more human footprints below the surface. 
NPS Photo

 For 80 years, only a small collection of fossilized footprints were known to exist at White Sands. However, in 2006, a group of scientists noticed dark spots dotting the expanse of the lakebed that appeared to be footprints. Their curiosities lead them to dig up these dark spots in 2009. This led to the discovery of both Harlan’s ground sloth and human footprints. During the 2010s, footprints of a dire wolf were discovered. These footprints were located next to ancient seeds. Scientists dated these seeds to more than 18,000 years ago.  
  
 In 2018, researchers discovered what they believe to be footprints of a female. They tell a story that may seem familiar today; her footprints show her walking for almost a mile, with a toddler’s footprints occasionally showing up beside hers. Evidence suggests that she carried the child, shifting them from side to side and occasionally setting the child down as they walked. The footprints broadened and slipped in the mud as a result of the additional weight she was carrying.   
  
 Based on stature and walking speed, it appears that most of the footprints in this study come from teenagers and children. As reported in the journal [Science](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.abg7586), “One hypothesis for this is the division of labor, in which adults are involved in skilled tasks whereas 'fetching and carrying' are delegated to teenagers. Children accompany the teenagers, and collectively they leave a higher number footprints that are preferentially recorded in the fossil record. This pattern is common to all excavated surfaces.” (Bennett, 2021)   
  
  

![Image 10: Artist rendition of ice age megafauna at different "time periods" showing mammoths, giant sloths, American camel, and human in a lush grassland landscape](https://www.nps.gov/whsa/learn/nature/images/Ice-Age-Megafauna-at-White-Sands_Karen-Carr.jpg?maxwidth=1300&maxheight=1300&autorotate=false&format=webp)

Showing the different “time periods” of the last ice age, and before the sand dunes formed, White Sands would have looked like a mix of grasslands and wetlands surrounding the great ancient Lake Otero. 
Karen Carr

![Image 11: In a scene from the ice age, a woman holding a child on the shores of the ancient Lake Otero leave the footprints in the mud.](https://www.nps.gov/whsa/learn/nature/images/WHSA-Adult-Child-Tracks-Web.jpg?maxwidth=650&autorotate=false)

In a scene from the ice age, a woman holding a child on the shores of the ancient Lake Otero leave the footprints in the mud. 
Courtesy of Karen Carr

 Footprints across White Sands have been found coexisting and interacting with extinct ice age animals. One set of footprints shows what appears to be humans stalking a giant sloth. This is demonstrated by human footprints being found inside the footprints of the sloth as they were tracked. Unfortunately for our hunter, there is no evidence that this was a fruitful hunt.  
  
 Although the reason for the disappearance of the great animals of the ice age is still debated, most theories do agree that climate change had a major influence. Environments once rich in lush green life began to disappear as those regions began experience less rainfall and higher temperatures. The fossilized footprints of White Sands are probably the most important resources in the Americas to understand the interaction of humans and extinct animals from the ice age.  
  
 These fossilized footprints, among other natural and cultural features found in the dunefield, further propelled the movement to re-designate White Sands National Monument into White Sands National Park. As a massive landscape filled with history, White Sands continually proves to be more than just a sandbox.  
  
[Dig Deeper: What animals made these tracks?](https://www.nps.gov/whsa/learn/nature/paleontology.htm)  

![Image 12: A park ranger taking a photo of two parallel paths of human footprints in compact white sand.  Fossilized human footprints of an adult and small child in compact white sand.](https://www.nps.gov/whsa/learn/nature/images/White-Sands-Human-Footprints-Adult-and-Child.png?maxwidth=1300&maxheight=1300&autorotate=false&format=webp)

NPS Photo

![Image 13: two visitors stand in hallways reading a sign in an alcove. Sands of Time is written on the top. Casted human footprints can be seen in front of the visitors.](https://www.nps.gov/whsa/learn/nature/images/IMG_5758.jpg?maxwidth=650&autorotate=false)

A brand new exhibit on the trackways at White Sands National Park was installed in the visitor center January of 2024. 
NPS Photo, Patrick Kark

 Currently the footprints at White Sands are inaccessible.   
  
 The park is continually working on ways to help visitors experience these incredible resources. One of these ways is updating broll footage and releasing images for the public as this story continues to evolve. These resources can be found below 
*   [B-roll Footage and interviews with researchers](https://www.nps.gov/whsa/learn/nature/footprintsmedia.htm)
*   [Fossilized Footprint Photo Gallery](https://npgallery.nps.gov/SearchResults/albumid/d10fdfcf-6597-4ced-a63e-8d221fc65a10)

  
 A new exhibit was installed at the visitor center in January of 2024 with more information and casted human footprints for visitors to enjoy and learn more about these trackways.
